Motion carries unanimously to close the meeting at 7:53 p.m. 2026-10-21 Planning Commission Meeting Minutes Draft TO: Augusta Township Planning Commission FROM: Joe Pezzotti, AICP Township Planner DATE: November 11, 2026 SUBJECT: Temporary Moratorium Ordinance and Process OVERVIEW On September 22, 2026, the Augusta Township Board of Trustees adopted Ordinance No. 2026-04, amending Article 14, “Administration and Enforcement” of the Township Zoning Ordinance to establish procedures for considering temporary zoning moratoriums. For this brief, Ordinance No. 2026-04 will also be known as the “Moratorium Ordinance.” The ordinance authorizes the Planning Commission to recommend temporary moratoriums to the Township Board when additional time is necessary to review and potentially amend existing zoning ordinance provisions. The ordinance establishes the findings, documentation, and procedural requirements necessary to forward such recommendations to the Township Board. During its past meetings, the Planning Commission has shown interest in recommending a temporary moratorium for high resource demand facilities, including data centers, to provide the Township with an opportunity to evaluate its existing zoning regulations and determine whether amendments are necessary to adequately address the potential impacts of these uses. The purpose of this memorandum is to outline the Planning Commission's responsibilities under Ordinance No. 2026-04 and identify the findings and supporting documentation necessary to forward a moratorium recommendation to the Township Board. ROLE OF THE PLANNING COMMISSION As outlined in Section II of Ordinance No. 2026-04, the Planning Commission is responsible for evaluating the need for a temporary moratorium and making a formal recommendation to the Township Board. The Planning Commission does not have the authority to independently impose a moratorium. Its responsibility is to establish a documented basis for the proposed moratorium and determine whether one is warranted. To accomplish this, the Planning Commission should: 1. Evaluate the potential impacts associated with high resource demand facilities and determine whether the zoning ordinance as it stands today adequately addresses those impacts. 2. Provide, review, and discuss relevant technical information, studies, professional opinions, and other available evidence. 3. Prepare a written Findings of Fact document, identifying the specific concerns and regulatory deficiencies supporting the proposed moratorium. 4. Create and review a draft moratorium ordinance establishing the uses, activities, and geographic areas to which the moratorium would apply. 5. Conduct a required public hearing and consider comments received. 6. Make a formal recommendation to the Township Board, supported by a majority vote of the Planning Commission. Benjamin R. Carlisle, President John L. Enos, Vice President Paul Montagno, Principal Megan Masson-Minock, Principal Laura Kreps, Principal Brent Strong, Principal David Scurto, Principal Sally M. Elmiger, Principal Craig Strong, Principal Douglas J. Lewan, Principal Richard K. Carlisle, Past President/Senior Principal R. Donald Wortman, Past Principal Temporary Zoning Ordinance Moratorium – High Resource Demand Facilities November 11, 2026 The Township Board is ultimately responsible for determining whether to adopt the proposed moratorium and is required to take into consideration the Planning Commission's findings and recommendations. REQUIRED FINDINGS OF FACT AND SUPPORTING DOCUMENTATION Section II of the Moratorium Ordinance identifies five (5) topics of consideration the Planning Commission should consider when evaluating the need for a temporary moratorium. The ordinance states the list is not comprehensive, and other additions may be added by either the Planning Commission or Township Board as part of the Findings of Fact document. 1. Infrastructure Strain The Planning Commission should evaluate whether high resource demand facilities could place significant demand or strain on existing public infrastructure, including electrical capacity, water supply, sewage disposal, drainage, and stormwater management. Supporting documentation may include utility capacity information, infrastructure assessments, anticipated resource demands, or comments from utility providers and other qualified professionals. 2. Public Safety Deficiencies The Planning Commission should consider whether existing infrastructure and emergency services are adequately equipped to accommodate the proposed uses in the event of an emergency. This may include roadway capacity, traffic circulation, emergency access, fire protection capabilities, and specialized emergency response needs. Supporting documentation may include input from the Fire Department, emergency service providers, transportation professionals, or other relevant agencies. 3. Zoning Regulatory Gaps The Planning Commission should identify specific deficiencies within the existing Zoning Ordinance that may prevent the Township from adequately reviewing or regulating high resource demand facilities. Potential considerations include whether existing requirements adequately address property and building setbacks, noise generation, screening and landscaping, site development standards, and decommissioning requirements. The findings should identify actual provisions or omissions (with section numbers) within the Zoning Ordinance that warrant further consideration, not general claims. 4. Master Plan Consistency The Planning Commission should evaluate whether high resource demand facilities are consistent with the Township's adopted Master Plan, Future Land Use Map, and long-term land use goals. The findings should consider whether additional zoning regulations are necessary to ensure that future development remains consistent with the Township's intended land use pattern. 5. Land Use Compatibility The Planning Commission should evaluate the potential compatibility of high resource demand facilities with surrounding properties and existing development patterns. Considerations may include proximity to residential properties, noise and visual impacts, environmental concerns, and other potential land use conflicts. The Planning Commission should also identify the specific zoning districts and/or geographic areas that would be subject to the proposed moratorium. 2 Temporary Zoning Ordinance Moratorium – High Resource Demand Facilities November 11, 2026 PUBLIC HEARING AND RECOMMENDATION Section VII of the Moratorium Ordinance explicitly requires each individual moratorium to be adopted through a separate zoning ordinance amendment. As a result, the Planning Commission must follow the applicable zoning amendment procedures under the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act and the Augusta Township Zoning Ordinance, which include noticing and holding a public hearing to hear public comment before making a recommendation to the Township Board. Following the required public hearing, the Planning Commission should consider the information presented, finalize its written findings, and determine whether to recommend the proposed moratorium. If the Commission determines that a moratorium is warranted, it should adopt a motion recommending approval and forwarding the following materials to the Township Board. The material to be forwarded with the motion should include: 1. 2. 3. 4. A written Findings of Fact document supporting the need for the moratorium. A draft moratorium zoning ordinance identifying its scope, applicability, and duration. The Planning Commission's formal recommendation, including any proposed modifications. Any additional supporting documentation considered by the Commission. The Township Board may review and modify the proposed moratorium ordinance and supporting findings, as appropriate, before making its final determination. DURATION AND LIMITATIONS Section V of the Moratorium Ordinance establishes a maximum initial moratorium period of six (6) months, with one potential extension not exceeding 90 days. The ordinance further requires the Township to make substantial, good-faith progress toward evaluating and potentially amending its zoning regulations during the moratorium period. A moratorium is intended to provide a temporary opportunity to address identified regulatory concerns. It is not intended to permanently prohibit a particular land use, target an individual applicant or property, or delay an application without pursuing the necessary zoning amendment process. These limitations should be considered when developing the proposed moratorium ordinance and the associated Findings of Fact. NEXT STEPS The Planning Commission should review the five areas identified in Section II of the Moratorium Ordinance and, following discussion amongst itself, determine whether findings can be established to support a temporary moratorium on high resource demand facilities. If the Planning Commission determines that the information discussed and documented supports the need for a moratorium, it should create/adopt its written Findings of Fact document and make a formal recommendation to the Township Board, accompanied by the proposed moratorium ordinance and supporting materials. Should the Commission determine that additional information is necessary to support its findings, it may postpone its recommendation until the appropriate documentation has been obtained and reviewed. Ultimately, the Planning Commission's responsibility is to provide the Township Board with a clear, factually supported recommendation demonstrating the need for a temporary moratorium and identifying the specific zoning deficiencies the Township needs to evaluate and address. 3 AUGUSTA CHARTER TOWNSHIP WASHTENAW COUNTY ORDINANCE 2026-05 TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON DATA CENTERS AND OTHER HIGH RESOURCE DEMAND FACILITIES EFFECTIVE: SEVEN DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION AFTER ADOPTION An Ordinance to make findings to protect the public health, safety, and welfare by establishing a temporary moratorium on data centers and other high resource demand facilities; to implement a temporary moratorium on applications for data centers and other high resource demand facilities; to provide a term for the temporary data center and other high resource demand facilities moratorium; to provide for severability; to repeal all ordinances or parts of ordinances in conflict therewith; and to provide an effective date. AUGUSTA CHARTER TOWNSHIP WASHTENAW COUNTY, MICHIGAN ORDAINS: SECTION I ZONING ORDINANCE TEXT AMENDMENT ARTICLE 14 – ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT In accordance with the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act, PA 110 of 2006, as amended, Augusta Charter Township has determined the following: Article 14, “Administration and Enforcement,” is hereby amended by adding Subsection 14.13(A), to be titled “Temporary Moratorium on Data Centers and High Resource Demand Facilities”, which subsection shall read as follows: SECTION II DEFINITIONS The following definitions shall apply to “Data Centers” and “High Resource Demand Facilities”: 1. Data Center: A facility used for centralized storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital information, typically containing computer servers, data storage systems, telecommunications equipment, power distribution systems, cooling and ventilation systems, uninterruptible power supplies, backup generators, and associated support infrastructure. The term includes colocation centers, cloud-computing facilities, hyperscale computing facilities, and similar high-intensity information technology operations. The term does not include small server rooms, IT closets, or similar equipment rooms that are clearly accessory and subordinate to another lawful principal use. 2. High Resource Demand Facility (HRDF): A principal nonresidential facility, campus, or group of buildings under common ownership or control that is characterized by (1) continuous or near-continuous operation, and (2) significant mechanical, electrical, or cooling infrastructure, and that meets the applicability criteria in subsections (A) and (B) below. A facility shall be considered an HRDF only when the criteria of both A and B below are met: a) Operational Characteristics. The facility includes one or more of the following operational characteristics that are integral to the primary use: 1. Central plant or large-scale mechanical cooling and/or ventilation systems serving process loads or IT/electronic equipment; 2. On-site emergency generation with an aggregate nameplate capacity exceeding 2,000 kW or 2 MW, and/or on-site fuel storage exceeding 10,000 gallons; 3. Dedicated electrical transformation/switchgear yard, substation, or similarly intensive electrical infrastructure primarily serving the facility; 4. 24-hour operations and/or operational necessity requiring uninterrupted environmental control (temperature/humidity) or high-reliability power systems. b) Resource/Infrastructure Thresholds. The facility exceeds one or more of the following thresholds, as demonstrated by applicant-prepared estimates and utility/service provider documentation, including any phased expansion approved or constructed within five (5) years: 1. Water demand: average daily water demand > 100 gpm; 2. Sanitary sewer: average daily sanitary discharge > 50,000 gallons/day; 3. Electric demand: maximum contracted demand or designed peak demand > 10 MW (or equivalent documented kW); 4. Hazardous materials / regulated wastes: storage, use, or generation requiring reporting under EPCRA Tier II and/or applicable state hazardous materials reporting and/or generation of hazardous waste at a level regulated under state/federal hazardous waste generator requirements, as documented on a materials inventory submitted with the application. SECTION III PLANNING COMMISSION FINDINGS The Augusta Charter Township Planning Commission has determined the following: 1. The Augusta Charter Township Planning Commission determines that the approval of data centers and other high resource demand facilities may result in or produce negative impacts on permitted land uses and development and may harm the public health, safety and general welfare of property owners and residents of the Township. 2. The Planning Commission is aware of significant public health, safety, and welfare concerns being raised by the public about the impacts of data centers and other high resource demand facilities. 3. The Township has a legitimate public purpose in assessing the regulation of the establishment and use of data centers and other high resource demand facilities within the Township to ensure that data centers and other high resource demand facilities do not interfere with other land uses, or have substantial negative impacts on the environment, public health, and safety. 4. The Planning Commission finds that adopting a temporary moratorium is reasonable and necessary for, among other reasons, the following: A. Michigan courts have recognized that a moratorium is a common and legitimate tool to preserve the status quo while formulating a development strategy. B. The adoption of a temporary moratorium would allow the Township Board and Planning Commission adequate time to study the public health, safety, and welfare concerns regarding data centers and other high resource demand facilities and allow for any needed Zoning Ordinance amendment and implementation process to occur, including attention to and consideration of citizen input and involvement, public debate, and full consideration of all issues and points of view. 5. The Planning Commission accordingly determines that it is desirable and in the public interest for the reasons set forth in its Findings of Fact documents attached hereto as “Exhibit A” to this ordinance and recommends that the Board adopt a temporary moratorium for data centers and other high resource demand facilities. SECTION IV DATA CENTER AND OTHER HIGH RESOURCE DEMAND FACILITIES MORATORIUM A temporary moratorium is imposed upon the acceptance and/or processing of any applications for data centers and other high resource demand facilities. This moratorium shall be subject to all applicable exemptions and hardship waiver provisions established under Section 14.13 of the Augusta Charter Township Zoning Ordinance. SECTION V TERM OF DATA CENTER AND OTHER HIGH RESOURCE DEMAND FACILITIES MORATORIUM The data center moratorium imposed by this Ordinance will remain in effect until 6 months after the effective date of this ordinance, or until amendments to the Zoning Ordinance regarding data centers and other high resource demand facilities become effective, whichever occurs first. No later than 60 days before this moratorium expires, the Township Board shall determine whether to initiate consideration of an extension, and if so, may extend the moratorium by ordinance as appropriate to allow additional time for Township review and consideration of the application, revision, review or repeal/replacement of zoning ordinance provisions. ULDRIKS DRIVE BATTLE CREEK, MICHIGAN ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS MEETING MINUTES September 9th, 2026 Call to Order: by Chairman Sprau at 6:00 pm Pledge of Allegiance administered by attending body Roll Call: Tom Sprau, Mark Thompson, Jim Barron, Sergio Orozco, Claudia Brown, 5 Members Present. Quorum Established. Approval of September 9th, 2026, Meeting Agenda: Commissioners received the meeting agenda in their packets. No other additions or deletions were suggested. It was moved by Commissioner Brown and Second by Commissioner Barron to approve the meeting agenda as presented. Roll Call 5 in favor/0 opposed. Motion Carries. Approval of July 13th, 2026, Meeting Minutes: Commissioners received a draft copy of the July 13", 2026, Zoning Board of Appeals Meeting Minutes. No other additions or deletions were suggested. It was moved by Commissioner Barron and Second by Commissioner Thompson to approve the meeting minutes. Roll Call 5 in favor/0 opposed. Motion Carries Building and Zoning Report: Zoning Administrator, Cody McCarty shared that the new check list for site plan requirements is now ready to be handed out to Applicants with applications. Additionally, he is working with the Planning Commission Chair to design an “application for wavier” that could waive stipulations if needed by the Planning Commission Chair only. We may have a SLU needing a variance coming our way in the near future. Public Comment Time: (Agenda Items Only) Open @ 6:08pm Close @ 6:08pm — With No Comments Discussion: Section 13.05 Variances and Appeals: 13.05 B 4 a— 1-5: Open discussion regarding the criteria that must be met in order to prove a hardship. The difference between Use and Non-Use Variances. Understanding “Conditions of Approval”. Discussion of the 90-day rule. Public Comment time: Open @6:28pm Close @ 6:28pm - With no comments ZBA Member Time: Chairman Sprau: inquired how often the ZBA meet? Discussion ensued among members with a unanimous decision that Quarterly is best. Inquired about the process of recruiting two alternates and if we need them immediately. Discussion revealed that we don’t need them immediately, but we need to investigate that further down the road. Commissioner Barron: Shared that he splits his time between Michigan and North Carolina but will be in attendance as much as possible. He also asked if you could attend the meetings virtual? The Zoning Administrator responded with probably not, but will reach out to Legal Counsel for verification. Chairman Sprau moved to adjourn the meeting at 6:39pm. Next Meeting November 9" , 2026, at 6:00pm Tom Sprau, Chair Claudia Brown, Secretary Charter Township Of Bedford Zoning Board of Appeals Meeting Dates for 2027 Tentative Dates Feb 3'—- Wed May 3 - Mon Aug 3" - Tues Nov 3 —- Wed OR Feb 1° — Mon May 3 - Mon Aug 2"? - Mon Nov 1**- Mon Charter Township Of Bedford Zoning Board of Appeals Rules for Public Comment & Decorum . The Chair will recognize all individuals wishing to speak during public comment time. . No person shall address the Zoning Board of Appeals without first being recognized by the Chair. . To provide for orderly public comment, each public comment submitted to the Zoning Board of Appeals made by an individual shall be limited to three (3) minutes in duration, unless extended by agreement of the presiding member of the Zoning Board of Appeals. . Allcomments shall be made from the speaker’s podium and any individual making comments shall first give their name. . The first public comment time is limited to agenda items only. The last public comment may be on any topic of interest or concern to the individual speaking. . Public comment is NOT a question-and-answer period. It provides individuals with an opportunity to express concerns, opinions, or questions to the Zoning Board of Appeals. All comments should be directed to the presiding member of the Zoning Board of Appeals. . The Zoning Board of Appeals will not respond to comments made during the public comment period unless it becomes necessary to ask a Clarifying question, immediately correct a factual error, or provide specific additional information. The ZBA members may choose to address certain public comments during their personal privilege/announcement time at the end of the meeting. . There will be no demonstrations during or at the conclusion of anyone’s remarks or presentations. . The Zoning Board of Appeals authorizes the Chair to: > Interrupt, warn or terminate an individual’s public comment when the comment exceeds three (3) minutes. > Request that any individual leave the meeting and/or request the assistance of law enforcement officers in the removal of such individual, when such individual’s conduct is a breach of the peace by interfering with the orderly progress of the meeting, pursuant to MCL 15.263 (6) of the Open Meetings Act; and > Call for a recess or an adjournment to another time if an individual’s lack of public decorum creates an environment in which the Zoning Board of Appeals is unable to conduct the business before it.

Return to Agenda To: Eaton County Local Units of Government From: Ben Dawson, Controller/Administrator Subject: Eaton County Local Tax Defense Fund On October 21, 2026, the Eaton County Board of Commissioners adopted the Local Tax Defense Fund (LTDF) Policy, establishing a $100,000 fund to help local units of government cover the cost of defending property tax appeals. This letter is to make sure your community knows the funds are available and how to use them. Property tax appeals, especially from large commercial and industrial property owners, can be expensive to defend. When an appeal succeeds, the reduction in taxable value is permanent. It lowers revenue for your community, schools, and every other taxing unit, and too often shifts the burden onto homeowners and small businesses. The Board created this fund so that no local unit has to weigh a strong defense against what it can afford. HOW THE FUND WORKS The Board allocated $100,000 to the LTDF for fiscal year 2026/27 (October 1, 2026 – September 30, 2027) from Unassigned General Fund Balance above the County's 15% target, under Resolutions #26-7-119 and #26-7-120. Future funding, if any, will be set by the Board each year during the budget process. Eligible defense costs are the direct costs your community pays to defend a property tax appeal, including: • Legal services • Appraisal costs • Expert witness fees • Other direct costs of the defense REIMBURSEMENT LIMITS Limit County Reimbursement Rate Maximum Per Request Maximum Per Approved Defensive Action Cumulative Cap Per Local Unit1 1 Amount Up to $10,000 for each $50,000 in eligible expenses $10,000 $30,000 $50,000 Cumulative Cap Per Local Unit resets each fiscal year. All reimbursements are subject to the balance remaining in the fund. If the fund is depleted, the Controller/Administrator may bring additional requests to the Board of Commissioners for consideration. The City of Lansing portion of Eaton County is not eligible except with the written approval of the Controller/Administrator. REQUESTS PROCESS Return to Agenda 1. Submit a written request to the Eaton County Controller’s Office 2. Submit proof of eligible expenses your community has already paid (invoices, proof of payment, etc.) 3. The Controller/Administrator, or their designee, will review the request If your community later receives a settlement covering the expenses of the appeal, the County’s reimbursement must be repaid in full. Repaid funds return to the LDTF to help other communities. LTDF funding is evaluated annually and there is not a guarantee for future support. If you currently have an appeal pending, or expect one, I encourage you to contact my office as soon as you can. If you have any questions, please reach out to my office at communication@eatoncounty.org. Thank you for your work protecting the tax base our residents depend on. Best regards, Ben Dawson Controller/Administrator Supervisor Fonda J. Brewer Clerk Mary R. Clark Treasurer Dennis R. Fedewa Manager Brian T. Reed Trustee Elizabeth S. Bowen Trustee Andrea M. Brewer and the Delta Township Board From: Hayden James, Associate Planner Peter Menser, Planning & Economic Development Director Date: November 9, 2026 Subject: Schools on Primary Roads Zoning Amendment – Final Adoption At its October 19, 2026 meeting, the Delta Township Board approved for introduction a zoning amendment to remove the requirement for public and nonpublic schools to have primary site access on a county primary road or state trunkline. The amended section would read as follows: SECTION 8.47 PRIMARY/SECONDARY SCHOOLS A. Ingress and Egress: Primary access to the subject parcel shall be on a county primary road, as classified by the Eaton County Road Commission, or on a state trunk line under the jurisdiction of the Michigan Department of Transportation. A. Setbacks: The minimum front setback for any principal or accessory building from a property line shall be fifty (50) feet, and the minimum side and rear setbacks shall be forty (40) feet. Parking areas shall provide a minimum setback of thirty (30) feet. Primary/Secondary Schools located completely within the Office (O) or Commercial (C) zoning districts may be reduced to comply with the minimum required setbacks mandated for principal buildings, accessory buildings, and parking lots within these districts. Greater setbacks may be required when abutting or facing residentially zoned properties. B. Parking: Parking areas shall not be located in any required setback areas. C. Play Areas: Outdoor play areas shall not be permitted in the required front setback area. D. Service and Maintenance Buildings: Buildings used for servicing or maintenance, such as heating plants, garages, and storage structures, shall be screened from residentially zoned properties in accordance with the standards of Section 12.02 herein. Since the last meeting staff published the required legal notice announcing introduction of the proposed zoning amendment. Staff suggests the following motion to approve the proposed zoning amendment for final adoption: “I move that the Delta Township Board approve for final adoption the proposal to amend Section 8.47 of the Zoning Ordinance to remove subsection 8.47(A), which requires that public and nonpublic schools have primary access on a primary road, as classified by the Eaton County Road Commission, or a state trunkline under the jurisdiction of the Michigan Department of Transportation. Call to the Public: None 7. Old and New Business a. Site Plan Application #26-011 Proposed facade and site renovations at 10440 Highland Road Director Langer stated the following:  Gave an overview of the location and scope of the request: east of US 23, south side of M-59. Currently there is a BP fuel station.  Applicant is representing Meijer who intends to acquire the site and make it a Meijer fuel station and convenience store.  Only approval needed for the re-branding is from the Planning Commission and staff for a Land Use Permit. Joe Wright, PLA at Fishbeck; representing the Applicant, James Perry of Meijer; stated the following:  Site will be the Meijer Express Fuel and Convenience Store.  Minimal changes to the site itself, with significant changes to the exterior and interior layout.  Intend to update the landscaping.  Intend to add gates to the dumpster enclosure.  Smoothie King will remain as a tenant. Chair Fox referred to the staff memorandum dated October 1, 2026. Brands change often; why is this coming before the Planning Commission? 2 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES OCTOBER 8, 2026 – 7:00 PM Director Langer stated the following:  Adding height to the building façade and adding some knee-walls on the west side.  Current owner came to the Planning Commission to refurbish the building. At that time outdoor storage and screening was discussed. Meijer stated they will take care of the existing outdoor storage by adding proper screen walls.  Landscape changes. SITE PLAN REVIEW – Applicable Site Standards Landscaping and Screening Director Langer stated  Site needs some attention but a change in occupancy does not require a landscaping review.  Meijer expressed a desire to address the need for landscaping; updating and cleaning it up.  Staff continues to work with Meijer. Commissioner Grissim commented what is being suggested is great. Rather than trees and evergreen yews on the east side of the parking area that will be impacted by vehicles, maybe ornamental grasses might be easier to maintain. The Applicant agreed and stated they also intend to irrigate the site. The Applicant also stated the following:  Added a sidewalk and concrete on the west side so they could put the ice chest and propane cage on the west side; there will be a knee wall for screening.  Intend to replace concrete façade in front; Meier wants a clean slate visual in front.  Fuel tank replacement will require some trenching; rather than patching the asphalt, they intend to mill and repave that area.  Will look very new. Lighting (Section 5.13) Director Langer stated the following:  Some values exceed the maximum footcandles permitted and some information is missing, which is not uncommon but easily addressed: the lighting under the awnings (north side of the building) should be included in the footcandle values/intensity calculations on the photometric plan.  Fuel canopy eyebrow lighting shown on the photometric plan is not permitted and details should be removed from the photometric plan (Luminaire schedule and detail A1).  Need to add the fixture type under the awning on the north side.  The photometric plan shall be revised to address comments in this section on the Construction Plan set. Commissioner McMullen commented she feels it is dark there now and would like it to be brighter so people will feel safer. Architecture / Building Materials Director Langer stated the following: Convenience store renovations  Keeping the building materials but providing additional colors. Hartland Township Page 2 Updated 10/28/26 3 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES OCTOBER 8, 2026 – 7:00 PM  Adding about five (5) feet to the entryway.  Dumpster will be painted to match the building. Fueling Station Canopy Renovations  Colored band on the canopy is slightly too large and must be adjusted.  Sigs are part of a different review. Outdoor storage area and screen wall  Increasing the concrete within the proposed screened outdoor storage area on the west side of the building.  Outdoor storage is permitted if properly screened. Dumpster gates  Four (4) new wood gates are to be added to the existing dumpster enclosure. Commissioner Mitchell asked about the changes requested since the Site Plan Review Committee met. The Applicant stated the changes were not incorporated into this plan. The Applicant wanted the Planning Commission to know they did not ignore the request of the SPRC and did share those changes, but the design team asked that the Applicant once again explain the thickness of the band and the eyebrow lighting are considered branding elements for Meijer. The Applicant stated they understand what is permitted and will comply. Director Langer stated since this is not a Planned Development, the Applicant really does not have any other option than to meet the ordinance requirements. Commissioner Grissim offered the following Motion: Move to approve Site Plan Application #26-011, a request to renovate the exterior façade of the multi-tenant commercial building and update selective site elements at 10440 Highland Road, as outlined in the staff memorandum dated October 1, 2026. Approval is subject to the following conditions: 1. The applicant shall adequately address the outstanding items noted in the Planning Department’s memorandum, dated October 1, 2026, on the Construction Plan set, subject to an administrative review by the Planning staff prior to the issuance of a land use permit. 2. A land use permit is required prior to the commencement of the exterior façade renovations and/or applicable site improvements as shown on the site plans. 3. Signs are not approved as part of this request. The blue accent stripe on each of the four (4) sides of the fueling station canopy is not approved as part of this request. Signs and the blue accent stripes require separate sign permits which are subject to an administrative review by the Planning staff. 4. Applicant complies with any requirements of the Township Engineering Consultant, Department of Public Works Director, the Fire Code requirements, and all applicable government agencies as applicable. Seconded by Commissioner Murphy. Hartland Township Page 3 Updated 10/28/26 4 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES OCTOBER 8, 2026 – 7:00 PM Commissioner Mayer inquired if the changes needed to be added as conditions. Director Langer replied no, it has been addressed. Motion carried unanimously. b. Comprehensive Development Plan 5 Year Review Director Langer stated the following;  Any municipality is required to review their Master Plan/Comprehensive Development Plan every five (5) years.  Thought was to review them in a joint session with the Township Board but have been unable to secure a date.  Hoping to have someone come in and speak to give real information regarding data centers and other topics of concern.  Under a time limit for this review; the Director has composed a memorandum for the Planning Commission and the Township Board to review to meet the requirement.  Memorandum includes links to all of the documents.  Also included a checklist from Michigan State University Planning Extension. Commissioner Eckman asked when the Comprehensive Plan was last completely reviewed. Commissioner Grissim responded 2004. Director Langer added there was an amendment in 2015 and another in 2020-2021 following the Retail Market Analysis. There has been discussion about updating the existing plan with new demographic information, but no date has been set for that review. It can be a long process. Chair Fox stated much of the existing plan is historical and does not need to be updated. The Future Land Use Map was reviewed and some adjustments made. Commissioner Eckman stated the real power of the plan is the Future Land Use Map. The Planning Commission discussed the process. Commissioner Eckman offered the following Motion: Move to recommend that the Planning Commission determine that the five-year review of the Comprehensive Development Plan has been completed and that no amendments to the Plan are necessary at this time. Findings: 1. The overall goals and objectives of the Comprehensive Development Plan remain applicable to the Township’s current planning and development needs. 2. The Future Land Use Map continues to provide reasonable guidance for anticipated land use and development patterns 3. Development and redevelopment activity since the adoption of the Comprehensive Development Plan has not identified a substantial conflict with the Plan’s overall land use policies. Site Plan Application #26-008 for a proposed financial institution with drive-through service (Hartland Towne Square Planned Development) Director Langer stated the following:  Gave an overview of the location and scope of the request: located east of US 23, north of M59 in the Hartland Towne Square development, west of Buffalo Wild Wings.  New building for Financial Plus Credit Union.  Requires Site Plan approval only from the Planning Commission. Representing the Applicant, Jeff Beymer of DEI Inc., and Sean Freeley of Financial Plus Credit Union introduced themselves and stated they are excited to bring this project to Hartland Township. Chair Fox referred to the staff memorandum dated October 15, 2026. Impact Assessment Chair Fox stated an Impact Assessment is not required. Director Langer explained when Hartland Towne Square was developed an impact statement was provided at that time that included the entire development. The different applicants for the various businesses in the development have not been required to submit a separate impact assessment. Traffic Generation Chair Fox stated it is the same as the Impact Assessment. Director Langer concurred. 7 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES OCTOBER 22, 2026 – 7:00 PM Access and Circulation Chair Fox stated the site is accessed from a proposed driveway from Hartland Square Drive and an internal access drive that connects to Buffalo Wild Wings on the east and a vacant parcel on the west. Site Requirements Barrier-Free Parking (Per ADA guidelines and approved Pattern Book – Page 44) Director Langer referred to the site plan indicated a barrier-free parking space shown at five (5) feet wide rather than eight (8) feet wide as required. The neighboring space is eleven (11) feet wide but does not need to be so there is room to make this change without impacting the number of spaces. Director Langer also mentioned the site plan indicates ten (10) spaces in the same area where the Landscape Plan only shows nine (9). They need twenty-two (22) and the site plan shows twentytwo (22). If the Applicant desires to keep the larger endcaps for more landscaping, they will need a waiver for the one (1) parking space. The Planning Commission and the Applicant briefly discussed their parking needs. The Planning Commission granted a waiver for the one (1) parking space for a total of twenty-one (21) spaces. Loading (Per approved Pattern Book – Page 41) Chair Fox stated a designated loading space is not typically required for this type of project. Landscaping Commissioner Grissim stated the following:  Difference in Site Plan and Landscape Plan has been resolved.  Screen parking with Evergreen Shrubs.  Visited the site to view the Pear Trees, some in the area have a disease but those looked great for now.  Shifting trees around, there is plenty of room.  Show the light poles on the Landscape Plan. Public Hearing: Bachman Trust, PZBA2026-02, Parcel #s: 4706-24-100-013, 4706-24-100-011 Article VI SFR – Single Family Residential, Section 6.06 – Dimensional Requirements Except as Otherwise Specified in this Ordinance: Variance request to create a parcel with less than 120 feet of lot width / road frontage Chairman Frenger opened the public hearing and read the instructions. Dan Davenport 6870 Grand River, Brighton, Michigan 48814 for the Bachman Trust requested that the property be split into 8 parcels. The parent parcel was purchased in 1956. Proposed parcel #1 has road access at the intersection of Monterey Court and Edgemont Drive. The existing width (54.27 feet) of Public Road frontage can support a driveway for a single-family residence. Driveway Site distance has been approved by Livingston County Road Commission. The 66 feet width of the parcel is not the width of the public road frontage. The split into individual parcels still requires review and approval by the Township Planning Commissioners. Call to the Public: David Dean Wade 800 East Allen Road – Email No Objection Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft Davita J. Finley 2467 Fisher Road -Handwritten note on Notice of Public Hearing letter in opposition to the request Staff Report Finding of Facts The Ordinance currently requires the following: • Section 26.02-C: The required minimum area and road frontage for each lot, parcel, or site area shall be equal to the minimum lot or parcel width as required in each zoning district. • As shown in the zoning map, these parcels are in the Single- F a m i l y Residential • Zoning District. Section 6.06-C: Minimum of 120 feet for a one (1) acre or more parcel and a minimum of 70 feet for 10,000 square feet to less than (1) acre parcel. As proposed, parcel 1 is a 13.19-acre parcel with 1.75 acres of upland area and would have, according to the survey, 54.27 feet of road frontage, meeting neither the 120-foot nor the 70-foot requirement for Single Family Residential parcels: The Township has historically read the deﬁnition of Building Setback Line to mean that a structure cannot be built on a parcel unless it is sited on the property outside of the parcel setbacks and meets the building setback line standard of the Zoning Ordinance. It is common for parcels in the Township to not have the required road frontage required in the Ordinance. An example of this is a parcel that does not have road frontage, but has an easement for ingress and egress, which is usually at most 66 feet wide, but is usually less. Another nearby example is a parcel that is a ﬂag Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft lot, which has a tail of property connecting the larger portion of the parcel to Fisher Road that is approximately 20 feet wide for their driveway, but which structure meets the property setbacks and the building setback line requirements. While the applicant also raises the deﬁnition of Lot, Waterfront in defense of the request, this deﬁnition does not apply to this request due to the deﬁnitions of Lot, and Lot of Record, because Parcel 1 does not yet exist and is therefore not a Lot of Record. Deﬁnitions: • Building Setback Line: The line formed by the outer surface of a structure or enclosure wall at or with the ﬁnish grade or surface of the ground; pertaining to and deﬁning those minimum (building) setback lines which are established, in general, parallel to the front road right-of-way line and within which setback area no part of a building shall project or be located, except as otherwise provided for by this Ordinance. • Building Line: A line formed by the face of the building, and for the purposes of this Ordinance, a minimum building line is the same as the front setback line. • Lot: A portion of land divided in conformance with all of the provisions of Public Act 288 of 1967 in accordance with Public Act 288 Land Division Act of 1967 as amended, Subdivision Control Act and the Subdivision Regulations of Howell Township. • Lot of Record: A lot existing prior to the adoption of this Ordinance and recorded in the office of the County Register of Deeds. For the purposes of this Ordinance, land contracts and purchase options not recorded in the County Register of Deeds’ Office but dated and executed prior to the effective date of the Ordinance shall also constitute a “lot of record”. (Includes “Parcel of Record”) • Lot, Waterfront: A lot having a frontage directly upon a lake, river or other reasonably sized impoundment of water. The portion adjacent to the water shall be designated as the lake frontage of the lot, and the opposite side shall be designated the road frontage of the lot. • Road Frontage: The legal line of demarcation between a dedicated road right-of-way or easement and abutting land. • Road Line: The line which forms the outer limits of a road right-of-way or easement, and which forms the line from which all road setbacks and front yards are measured. Zoning Ordinance Standards For the ZBA to approve a dimensional variance the applicant must demonstrate a practical difficulty. The ZBA should review the documents submitted by the applicant supporting the variance request against the provisions of the Ordinance, Section 22.07: 1. That special conditions and circumstances exist which are peculiar to the land use, land, structure or building in the same zoning district. • Parcel 4706-24-100-013 is an odd shape, including a road stub off Edgemont Drive. It appears that a much larger development was anticipated that would extend Edgemont Drive through the existing parcel to Pineway Trail allowing for more parcels and more homes to be built. The proposed lot is also an odd shape. While the proposed parcel may not meet the strict letter of the Ordinance, it meets the Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft spirit of the Ordinance by providing access to a public road no less than 20 feet in width, as required by Section 26.03 and 26.13. 2. That literal interpretation of the provisions of this Ordinance would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties in the same zoning district under the provisions of this Ordinance. • As stated above, there are a lot of parcels in the Township that have no road frontage, only an easement, or have less than the building setback line frontage as road frontage but still have the required access to a public road. 3. That granting of the variance requested will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by the provisions of this Ordinance to other lands, structures, or buildings in the same zoning district. • It is common in the Township for property to have less than the building setback line amount of road frontage. 4. That no nonconforming uses of other lands, structures, or buildings in the same zoning district, and not permitted use of lands, structures or buildings in other zoning districts, shall be considered grounds for the issuance of a variance. 5. Applicants shall also follow the outline of requirements prescribed by the Zoning Board of Appeals when applying for an appeal for an interpretation of or a variance from the provisions or requirements of this Zoning Ordinance. 6. Reasons set forth in the application justify the granting of the variance, and the variance is the minimum variance that will make possible the reasonable use of the land, building, or structure in the zoning district in which it is located. • The road stub from Edgemont Drive already exists and is over 20’ wide which is enough for access for a single driveway making the request larger than the minimum. 7. The granting of the variance will be in harmony with the general purpose and intent of this Ordinance, and will not be injurious or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare of the zoning district in which it is to be located. • One additional residential driveway on Edgemont Drive will be in harmony with the Ordinance and will not be detrimental to any existing property or owners in this residential area. Respectfully submitted, Jonathan Hohenstein Howell Township Zoning Administrator Motion by Counts, Second by Weaver, “I move that the Zoning Board of Appeals approve the request of Dan Davenport, on behalf of the Bachman Trust, for a dimensional variance from Sections 6.06(C) and 26.02(C) of the Zoning Ordinance to permit proposed Parcel 1, to be split from Parcel No. 4706-24-100-013, to have 54.27 feet of road frontage where 120 feet is required in the ordinance, with access to Edgemont Drive provided by an exclusive private driveway easement, based on the application materials, the Zoning Administrator’s staff report, and the testimony and evidence presented at the hearing, for the following reasons: The Applicant has demonstrated a practical difficulty because, due to the irregular shape of the parent parcel and proposed Parcel 1, including the existing road stub off Edgemont Drive, the width Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft of proposed Parcel 1 is not located along its public road frontage, making strict compliance with the road frontage requirement of Section 26.02(C) unnecessarily burdensome. In compliance with Section 22.07(A), the applicant has shown that there are special conditions and circumstances associated with the irregular shape of the parent parcel and proposed Parcel 1, including the existing road stub off Edgemont Drive, within the Single-Family Residential District that make it difficult to comply with Section 26.02 of the Zoning Ordinance. In compliance with Section 22.07(A)(2), applicant has shown that the literal interpretation of the ordinance would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties in the Single Family Residential District because there are other parcels within this district that have no road frontage, only an easement, or have less than the building setback line frontage as road frontage but still have required public road access, example Flagpole Lots. In compliance with Section 22.07(A)(3), the applicant has shown that the granting of the variance will not confer any special privilege that is denied to others within the same zoning district because it is common for properties within the Single-Family Residential to have less than the building setback line amount of road frontage. In compliance with Section 22.07(A)(4), no nonconforming uses of other lands, structures, or buildings in the district, and no permitted uses of lands, structures, or buildings in other zoning districts, have been considered as grounds for the issuance of this variance. In compliance with Section 22.07(B), applicant has followed the outline of requirements prescribed by the Zoning Board of Appeals in applying for this variance. In compliance with Section 22.07(C), subject to the conditions set forth below, the variance is the minimum variance that will make possible the reasonable use of the land in the SFR District because the variance is limited to proposed Parcel 1 and the exclusive driveway easement will be limited in width, which provides access to a public road consistent with Sections 26.03 and 26.13. In compliance with Section 22.07(D), the granting of the variance will be in harmony with the general purpose and intent of the Zoning Ordinance and will not be injurious or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare within the Single Family Residential District because one additional residential driveway on Edgemont Drive has minimal to no impact on the surrounding properties, including the adjoining parcels currently owned by the applicant, and the Livingston County Road Commission has recommended approval.” Roll Call: McEvoy- yes, Weaver- yes, Countsyes, Frenger- yes, Williams- yes. Motion passed (5-0). B. Jason Howe, PZBA2026-03, Parcel #: 4706-01-200-022 Article XIV- Supplemental Regulations, Section 14.07- Accessory Structures: Variance request to exceed the maximum square footage for an accessory building on a parcel less than 20 acres in size, as well as a dimensional variance to allow the accessory building to be located in front of the rear line of the property. Steve Brock, presented for Jason Howe, who was present but ill, not allowing him to speak easily. Mr. Howe owns 18.76 acres of land. With the passing of his father Mr. Howe has inherited several large pieces of agricultural pieces of equipment. Therefore, he desires to construct an accessory building to store these pieces of equipment. The dimensions of the building are 40 feet by 80 feet with a square footage of 3,200 feet. This is more than 3,000 square feet specified in the ordinance. There are 2 chicken coops, and a garage which places the square footage in excess by 2,009 square feet. Alternatives of attaching the garage and making chicken coups are not structural but found not to be feasible. Discussion Centered on the position of the accessory building. This was determined by geography and avoidance of proximity to power lines. (Not High voltage power lines). The position of the building made sense with respect to the topography of the property ZBA then focused on the size of accessory building with respect to the parcel size 18.76 acres. Matt Counts pointed out 3,000 square foot buildings were different from 3,000 square foot buildings on 20 acres. Discussion of the issue of whether this ordinance made sense. This was tabled to discuss after the Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft deliberation. Call to Public: None Staff Report Applicant: Jason Howe Property: 5937 Fisher Rd., Howell, MI 48855. Parcel# 4706-01-200-022 Request The owner of the property would like to construct a 3,200 square foot barn to house vehicles, and farm equipment located four feet in front of the rear line of the house. Background Jason Howe purchased the property in 2011. The parcel is approximately 18.76 acres and is located in the Agricultural Residential (AR) zoning district on the corner of Fisher Road and East Allen Road. Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft Findings of Fact Variance #1 Jason is requesting to construct an accessory structure that exceeds the square footage permitted under the Ordinance. The Ordinance currently limits the maximum square footage of Accessory buildings on parcels with less than 20 acres in the Agricultural Residential zoning district to 3,000 square feet. Section 14.07 C: Accessory Buildings located on lots and parcels in all Zoning Districts shall be subject to the following regulations: Jason’s proposed structure meets the definition of a detached accessory structure (see definition below), since it is not attached to the main house and will be used to store cars and farm equipment. It would be subject to the maximum square footage allowed of 3,000 square feet of accessory structures or 4% of lot area. Historically the Township has used the more restrictive regulation. There are currently four small accessory structures that total approximately 337 square feet and a detached garage that is 1,472 square feet for a total of 1,809 square feet of current accessory structures. Jason’s drawings indicate that the proposed accessory structure is 80’ x 40’ or 3,200 square feet. Jason’s application indicates he is asking for a 1,136 square foot variance but our calculations indicate it would be a 2,009 square foot variance that would be required. Building, Accessory. A supplementary building or structure on the same lot or parcel of land as the main building or buildings or part of the main building occupied by or devoted exclusively to any accessory use; but such use shall not include any building used for dwelling, residential or lodging purposes, or sleeping quarters for human beings except for these dwellings or residential buildings specifically permitted in this ordinance. Variance #2 Jason is also asking for a variance to allow the structure to be located four feet in front of the rear line of the principal dwelling. Section 14.07 B: Detached accessory buildings and structures shall be located entirely in the rear yard outside of the rear setback… There are exceptions to the rule, but they do not apply to this request. Secretary Lollio questioned who holds the responsibility for maintaining and inspecting Pineway Trail. Board Representative Boal questioned if the engineers report is sufficient because there is no mention of the Road Commission’s standards and if the agreement has been reviewed and approved by the Township Attorneys. Chairman Williams questioned why some of the parcels will be hooking up to city water and sewer, but others need a drain field. Commissioner Alchin recused himself from voting due to a potential conflict of interest. Motion by Boal, Second by Bonello, “To approve the partitioning to request further partitioning of Pineway Trail, the Bachman Trust PC2026-12, property #’s 4706-24-100-011 and -013 as the ends.” Motion carried. 2. PC2026-15: Pineview Village Phase ll, JMF Brewer LLC, 4706-27-200-014, Final Site Plan ReviewPlanner Montagno gave a brief synopsis of the project and answered questions. The layout has not changed from the previously approved Preliminary Site Plan. There are no outstanding issues, however it is recommended the Planning Commission require property line adjustments. Brent LaVanway from Boss Engineering representing JMF Brewer, presented details on the proposed development. The project includes 24 ranch-style units, public water service, private sewer grinder pump systems, garage-mounted coach lighting designed to minimize dark-sky impact and the preservation of a 300- foot existing vegetation buffer along Brewer Road. Board Representative Boal inquired about the requests from Livingston County Drain Commissions report, sewer grinder pumps, the drainage detention pond and property line adjustments. Commissioner Bonello asked whether purchasing property extending from Lucy Road has been considered to construct a cul-de-sac. Motion by Boal, Second by Lollio, “To approve the Final Site Plan Review for PC2026-15, Pineview Village Phase II, conditionally upon approval of the County Drain Commission, the Township Engineer, and MHOG.” Motion carried 3. PC2026-16: Soapy Bucket, 4706-25-200-048, Amendment to Site Plan- Planner Montagno summarized the revisions to the previously approved Preliminary Site Plan. The revised submission includes Phases 1A, 1 and 2. Phase 1A focuses on utility installation within the road right-of-way and construction of the private road at the Oak Grove entrance, including the associated taper. Phase 1 covers private road construction, completion of underground utilities along the roadway, and the installation of temporary stormwater basins and roadway lighting. Phase 2 involves installation of the lift station and related equipment at the east end of the property. Patrick Cleary with Boss Engineering presented the project details and answered questions. Secretary Lollio inquired about the submitted plan sets. Board Representative Boal sought clarification on whether Final Site Plan approval was being requested specifically for Phases 1, 1A and 2 and whether the detention pond is still included in Phase 1. Motion by Stanley, Second by Boal with friendly amendments, “To approve PC2026-16, Soapy Bucket Amendment to Site Plan to add approval to Township Engineers and Drain Commission and all outside utilities.” Motion carried. 4. Updates/Changes to the Zoning Ordinance due to the new Land Division Ordinance- Planner Montagno reported on the changes to the Land Division Ordinance and answered questions. There was an amendment that passed to the Land Division Act to Section 108, which allows for a greater number of divisions of a parent parcel of 10 acres or less. The parent parcel could be divided into 10 parcels when previously it was only 4 parcels, divisions would still need to meet local ordinance requirements. He recommends putting together a private road ordinance that has requirements for storm water, maintenance and private road standards for access that would be approved by engineers and the Township Board. Commissioner Bonello questioned whether the regulation could remain as written, limiting those parcels to four splits and if an ordinance can be changed at any time. Board Representative Boal inquired how parcel splits would be handled if property frontage was located along major roads versus private roads and if there is a way to prevent driveways every 120 feet. Discussion followed. OLD BUSINESS: 1. High Impact Land Use/ Data Center Ordinance- Planner Montagno provided an overview of changes to the High- Impact Land Use and Special Land Use ordinances and answered questions. Focusing on revocation provisions, Special Land Use requirements, definitions, parking, performance standards and site plan requirements. Resident Research Committee members Kristin Dennison and Angela Barbash presented recommended edits and asked questions. Board Representative Boal questioned parking space requirements and whether fuel storage is currently regulated for other industries or businesses. Commissioner Alchin questioned the purpose of the Development Agreement. Vice Chairman Stanley inquired whether if the ordinance could be amended at any time. Chairman Williams questioned lighting requirements during build up versus during operation and under the revocation section if anyone who files a complaint would be required to be identified or present. Discussion followed CALL TO THE PUBLIC: Chuck Smith, 5136 Fleming Rd- Spoke on opposition of Data Centers Evelyn Redwine, 444 Inverness- Thanked the Board and Resident Research Committee for their work on the ordinance. Gary Bodurka, 2865 Byron Rd- Spoke on Article 14, sounds and vibrations ADJOURNMENT: Motion by Boal, Second by Bonello, “For adjournment.” Motion carried. text: AGENDA RICHFIELD TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION WEDNESDAY November 4, 2026 at 7:30 PM CALL TO ORDER 1. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE 2. ROLL CALL 3. APPROVAL OF AGENDA 4. PREVIOUS MINUTES (August 5th, 2026) 5. CORRESPONDENCE - Memo from Attorney Gildner & Township Board 6. PRESENTATIONS: a. 7. i. Proposed zoning ordinance amendment – Temporary Portable Storage containers. ii. Proposes zoning ordinance amendment – add section 1903 regarding moratoriums for new or emerging land uses that may impact the health, safety or welfare of Township residents or property. PUBLIC HEARINGS: a. 8. Zoning administrator Proposed zoning ordinance amendments for Temporary portable storage containers and moratoriums on emerging land uses that may impact the health, safety or welfare of Township residents or property. NEW BUSINESS: a. Planning Commission consideration of zoning ordinance amendment section 1719 – Temporary Portable Storage containers. b. Planning Commission consideration of zoning ordinance amendment; adding section 1903 – Moratoriums on certain emerging land uses. OLD BUSINESS: PUBLIC COMMENT: ZONING ADMINISTRATOR REPORT: COMMISSION COMMENTS: ADJOURNMENT: Richfield Township 5381 N State Road Davison, MI 48423-8595 Phone:(810)653-3564 • Fax:(810)653-6295 www.richfieldtwp.org Joseph M. Madore Supervisor Cheryl Campbell-Hoberg Clerk Brian Arnes Treasurer Don Harris Trustee John Minto Trustee Memorandum To: Board members Date: September 4, 2026 RE: Amendment to zoning ordinance – Moratoriums for emerging zoning matters ___ Background: The State of Michigan has taken control away from the local jurisdictions when it comes to siting and approving large scale renewable energy facilities (think Data centers, solar or battery installations, etc.) with the enactment of PA 233 and PA 234 of 2023. Here are links to those bills: https://legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2023-HB-5120 https://legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2023-HB-5121 Last week , the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approved an 873-acre solar project in Ingham County, marking the first project approved under the state’s new large-scale renewable energy siting process, PA 233. I’ve been working with Attorney Gildner to create a zoning/approval moratorium on any of these types of facilities. The moratorium is meant to give local jurisdictions more time to investigate and come up with ordinances to regulate these types of facilities during the moratorium. A moratorium period is up to 12 months, with a possible 6-month extension. Analysis: Our goal would be to use the time of the moratorium to adopt a compatible renewable energy ordinance (CREO). A CREO is an ordinance that provides for the development of utility-scale energy facilities within the local unit of government that is no more restrictive than provisions included in Section 226(8) of PA 233. If we adopt a CREO, the applicant must go through Richfield Township for approval and bypass the commission (MPSC). Recommendation: This matter is on the September agenda for discussion and to determine if we want to direct the PC to go forward with the PH process to amend the zoning ordinance by adding SECTION 1903 that was prepared by Mr. Gildner. If this new section is added to the zoning ordinance, then the Board could more easily adopt a moratorium period to provide more time to deal with special, emerging zoning circumstances if/when they arise. Joseph M. Madore Richfield Township Supervisor MICHIGAN TOWNSHIPS ASSOCIATION Member 201-120 Sub aqueous Area, High Water Elevation The high water elevation of a sub aqueous area shall be the highest of the following: 1) the highest known elevation reached by water as determined by an examination of soil and vegetative conditions, 2) the maximum water elevation caused by a 10-year storm event, or 3) the highest level established by law for bodies of water which have their levels established by law. 201-121 Swimming Pool Any permanent, nonportable structure or container located either above or below grade designed to hold water to a depth of greater than twenty-four (24) inches, intended for swimming bathing. A swimming pool shall be considered an accessory structure for purposes of computing lot coverage. 201-122 Temporary Outdoor Sale Temporary outdoor sales are sales which are conducted as part of an existing commercial operation outside the walls or screen enclosed yards of the building which houses the sale proprietor. Such sales shall be for a period of time not longer than one (1) month and shall not be conducted by any one establishment or form any one business location more than two (2) times in any six-month period. Temporary outdoor sales do not include residential yard sales or flea markets. 201-122 (a) Temporary Portable Storage Container Shall be defined as a container fabricated for the purpose of transporting freight or goods on a truck, railroad or ship, including cargo containers, shipping containers, storage units, or other portable structures that are placed on private property and used for storage of items, including, but not limited to, clothing, equipment, goods, household or office fixtures or furnishing, materials and merchandise. This definition will also include accessory buildings used for temporary storage. Temporary Portable Storage Containers also include, but not limited to storage box shipping containers, storage moving "pods", or any other similar portable storage containers, whether with or without wheels, and whether with or without a chassis. 201-123 Temporary Use or Temporary Building A use or building permitted to exist during a specified period of time under conditions and procedures as provided for in this Ordinance. (See Section 1103) 201-124 Township The Township of Richfield, Genesee County, Michigan. 36 RICHFIELD TOWNSHIP ORDINANCE NO. ___ An ordinance to amend Article XIX of the Township Zoning Ordinance by adding a new section 1903 regarding moratoriums. THE TOWNSHIP OF RICHFIELD ORDAINS: Section 1. Amendment of Article XIX of the Township Zoning Ordinance. The Township Board hereby amends Article XIX of the Township Zoning Ordinance by adding thereto a new Section 1903, entitled “Moratoriums,” to read as follows: SECTION 1903 1. MORATORIUMS Moratorium by Resolution. The Township Board, by resolution, may impose a temporary moratorium upon the review or issuance of any and all applications, permits, rezonings, licenses, or approvals for specific special or other new or emerging land uses in the Township if the Township Board desires to review, enact, or amend provisions of the master plan or zoning ordinance to regulate specific special or other new or emerging land uses that may impact the health, safety or welfare of Township residents or property. 2. Purpose and Findings. The resolution must state the purpose of the moratorium and include findings of the Township Board in support of the moratorium. 3. Length of Moratorium Any resolution adopted pursuant to this section must specify the length of the moratorium, which may not exceed twelve (12) months. The resolution may provide for one (1) extension of the moratorium, by resolution, for up to six (6) months. 3. Notice. Notice of the resolution must be published within seven (7) days of its adoption. The notice must include the following: (a) A summary of the resolution's effect. (b) The length of the moratorium and whether an extension is possible. (c) Section 2. Where the public may inspect the resolution enacting the moratorium. Effective Date. This Ordinance shall take effect 30 days following publication. At a regular meeting of the Board of Trustees for the Township of Richfield held on ___, 2026, ___ moved for adoption of the foregoing ordinance and ___ supported the motion. Voting for: Voting against: The Supervisor declared the ordinance adopted. ___ Joseph M.
