text: ARTICLE 29.00 General Procedures and Related Standards Section 29.01 -- Purpose The purpose of this Article is to provide procedures and related standards for the processing of all requests for Township action or review under the provisions of this Ordinance. Section 29.02 -- Site Plan Review/ Process A. Intent The site plan review procedures, standards, and required information in this Section are intended to provide a consistent and uniform method of review of proposed development plans, to ensure full compliance with the regulations and standards contained in this Ordinance and other applicable ordinances and laws, including the Michigan Building Code, as amended, to achieve efficient use of the land, to protect natural resources, and to prevent adverse impact on adjoining or nearby properties. It is the intent of these provisions to encourage cooperation and consultation between the Township and applicant so as to facilitate development in accordance with the Township's land use objectives. B. Site Plan Required 1. 2. Site Plan Required Except as provided in the following sub-section B.2, the development of any new use, the construction of any new structures, any change of an existing use of land or structure, and all other building or development activities shall require site plan approval pursuant to this Section. For example, site plan review shall be required for any of the following activities: a. Erection, moving, relocation, conversion or structural alteration to a building or structure to create additional floor space, other than a single family or two family dwelling. b. Any development which would, if approved, provide for the establishment of more than one principal use on a parcel, such as, for example, a single family site condominium or similar project where a parcel is developed to include two (2) or more sites for detached single family dwellings. c. Development of all non-single family residential uses permitted in single family districts and in agricultural districts. d. Any change in use that could affect compliance with the standards set forth in this Ordinance, other than for single-family residential uses. e. Expansion or paving of off-street parking involving five (5) or more spaces and/or a change in circulation or access for other than a single-family dwelling. f. Any excavation, filling, soil removal, mining or landfill, or creation of ponds, except as otherwise specified in sub-section B.2, item c. g. The development or construction of any accessory uses or structures, except for uses or structures that are accessory to a single family or two family dwelling. h. Any use or development for which submission of a site plan is required by the provisions of this Ordinance. Site Plan Not Required Notwithstanding the preceding sub-section 1, site plan approval is not required for the following activities: a. Construction, moving, relocating or structurally altering a single or two family home, including any customarily incidental accessory structure. b. Development of a principal permitted agricultural use, or the construction, moving, relocation or structural alteration of permitted agricultural structures, including any customarily incidental accessory structures. Williamstown Township Zoning Ordinance Page 29 - 1 Article 29.00 c. C. General Procedures and Related Standards Any excavation, filling, soil removal, mining, or creation of ponds that is less than one-half acre in area and less than fifty (50) cubic yards, provided that such activity is normally and customarily incidental to single family and agricultural uses described in this sub-section for which site plan approval is not required. Site Plan Review Applications and Procedures 1. Optional Pre-Application Conference In order to facilitate processing of a site plan in a timely manner, the applicant may request a pre-application site plan conference with the Township Supervisor or Planner. The purpose of such a conference is to provide information and guidance to the applicant that will assist in preparation of the site plan. The applicant need not present drawings or site plans at a pre-application conference, but even if drawings or site plans are presented, no formal action shall be taken on a site plan at a pre-application conference. At any time during the course of preparation of a site plan prior to submission of a formal application, the Township shall upon request provide information concerning the Zoning Ordinance procedures and standards. 2. Optional Conceptual Review by Planning Commission or Township Board An applicant may file a written request of conceptual review of a preliminary site plan by the Planning Commission or Township Board to evaluate the following: a. Relationship of the site to nearby properties; b. Density; c. Adequacy of landscaping, open space, vehicular drives, parking areas, drainage, and proposed utilities; and, d. Conformance with Township development policies and standards. Conceptual review fees shall be paid according to the fee schedule established by the Township Board. No formal action shall be taken on a site plan submitted for conceptual review, and neither the applicant nor the Planning Commission or Township Board shall be bound by any comments or suggestions made during the course of the conceptual review. 3. Submission of Site Plan for Formal Review In order to initiate formal review by the Planning Commission and Township Board, the applicant is required to submit the following materials to the Williamstown Township Hall: a. One (1) completed and signed copy of the Application for Site Plan Review, b. Three (3) individually folded copies and one (1) digital copy in pdf format of the site plan. c. Proof that the plan has been submitted for review to all appropriate affected governmental agencies, including but not limited to the Ingham County Road Department, County Drain Commission, County Health Department, Michigan Department of Transportation (if located on Grand River Avenue), Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy, Northeast Ingham Emergency Service Authority (NIESA), and any other agencies deemed appropriate by the Planning Commission or Township Board. d. The required review fee. These materials shall be submitted to the Township no later than noon twenty-one (21) calendar days prior to the Planning Commission or Township Board meeting at which the review is requested. 4. Distribution of Plans Upon submission of all required application materials, the site plan proposal shall be placed on the next open Planning Commission agenda for Preliminary Review. The site plans and application shall be distributed to appropriate Township officials for review, including, as deemed necessary, the Township Planner and/or Engineer. Williamstown Township Zoning Ordinance Page 29 - 2 Article 29.00 5. D. General Procedures and Related Standards Review by Township Planner The Township Planner shall review the plans to determine compliance with the Zoning Ordinance, and shall submit a written report, which shall identify issues which must be resolved as well as all required revisions necessary to obtain site plan approval. Review and Final Action 1. Initial Review At the first regular meeting at which a site plan proposal is considered, the Planning Commission shall identify major issues and must be resolved and other revisions necessary to obtain site plan approval. 2. Public Hearing Site plans involving uses that are subject to Special Land Use Approval may require a public hearing. After payment of appropriate fees, the Planning Commission will set the date of the public hearing, subject to the requirements in Section 29.03. 3. Request for Revisions Upon Preliminary Review of the site plan proposal, the Planning Commission may require the applicant to complete revisions and submit the plans for engineering review prior to formal action being taken. The applicant shall be given the opportunity to revise the plans and submit revised plans for further review. All required revisions must be completed, or the site plan will not be put on the agenda for Final Review. 4. Submission of Plans for Final Review Three (3) individually folded copies and one (1) digital copy of the revised plan in pdf format shall be submitted for final review at least twenty-one (21) calendar days prior to the Planning Commission meeting at which review is requested. The revised plan shall be distributed to appropriate Township officials for review. 5. Planning Commission Final Review and Recommendation The Planning Commission shall review the site plan proposal together with any public hearing findings and any requested reports and recommendations from the Building Inspector, Township Planner, and other reviewing agencies. The Planning Commission shall then make a recommendation to the Township Board, based on the requirements and standards of this Ordinance. The Planning Commission may recommend approval, approval with conditions, or denial, or they may table the proposal, as noted below. In the context of an overall site plan, the Planning Commission may find that it would be appropriate to modify the specific requirements of the Ordinance, so as to best satisfy the Standards for Site Plan Approval in sub- section F. Accordingly, in the course of recommending approval or approval with conditions, the Planning Commission may allow modifications to the specific zoning standards that deal with sidewalk location; exterior lighting type, height or intensity; dumpster location; number and location of parking spaces; landscaping and screening requirements; loading zone location; and, fence and wall height and location. Justification for all such modifications shall be set forth in the Planning Commission meeting minutes. a. Approval Upon determination that a site plan is in compliance with the standards and requirements of this Ordinance and other applicable ordinances and laws, the Planning Commission shall recommend approval. b. Approval Subject to Conditions Upon determination that a site plan is in compliance except for minor modifications, the Planning Commission may recommend that the Township Board impose reasonable conditions upon the approval of the site plan. The conditions for approval shall be identified and the applicant shall be given the opportunity to correct the site plan. The conditions may include the need to obtain variances or obtain approvals from other agencies. If a plan is subsequently approved by the Township Board subject to conditions, the applicant shall submit a revised plan with a revision date, indicating compliance with the conditions. The applicant must re-submit the site plan to the Township Board for final approval after conditions have been met, unless the Township Board waives its right to review the revised plan, and instead authorizes the Township Supervisor or the Building Inspector to review and approve the site plan after all required conditions have been addressed. The Township Board may also require that the Township Supervisor or the Building Inspector to submit the revised plan to the Planner and/or Engineer for review and approval. c. Denial Upon determination that a site plan does not comply with the standards and regulations set forth in this Article or elsewhere in this Ordinance or requires extensive revision in order to comply with said standards and regulations, the Planning Commission shall recommend denial. Williamstown Township Zoning Ordinance Page 29 - 3 Article 29.00 d. General Procedures and Related Standards Tabling Upon determination that a site plan is not ready for approval or rejection, or upon a request by the applicant, the Planning Commission may table consideration of a site plan until a later meeting. 6. Township Board Action Following receipt of the Planning Commission's recommendation, the application shall be placed on the agenda of the next scheduled Township Board meeting, unless otherwise requested by the applicant in writing and approved by the Township Board. The Township Board shall review the final plan, together with the findings of the Planning Commission, and any reports and recommendations from the Building Inspector, Township Planner, and other reviewers. In the case of a condominium project, the Master Deed and condominium bylaws shall also be subject to Township Board review and approval. The Township Board may table consideration of a site plan. However, upon completion of its review, the Township Board shall approve, approve with conditions, or deny a site plan proposal in accordance with the guidelines described previously in Section 29.02, sub-section D.5. An applicant shall have a maximum of two (2) years from the date of submittal of a site plan for formal review to achieve final Township Board approval. If approval is not achieved within this period, the application becomes null and void and a new application is required to pursue site plan review further. 7. Recording of Site Plan Review Action Each action taken with reference to a site plan review shall be duly recorded in the minutes of the Planning Commission or Township Board as appropriate. The grounds for action taken upon each site plan shall also be recorded in the minutes. After final action has been taken on a site plan and all steps have been completed, three copies of the application and plans shall be marked APPROVED or DENIED, as appropriate, with the date that action was taken. One marked copy will be returned to the applicant and the other two copies will be kept on file in the Township Hall. Furthermore, the Township shall file with the Ingham County Register of Deeds, an affidavit of site plan and/or special use approval, with conditions of approval. 8. Procedure After Site Plan Approval a. Application for Building Permit Following final approval of the site plan and the engineering plans, the applicant may apply for a building permit. It shall be the responsibility of the applicant to obtain all other applicable Township, County, State, or Federal permits prior to issuance of a building permit. A building permit for a structure in a proposed condominium project shall not be issued until evidence of a recorded Master Deed has been provided to the Township. However, the Building Official may issue permits for site grading, erosion control, installation of public water and sewage facilities, and construction for roads prior to recording the Master Deed. No permit issued or work undertaken prior to recording the Master Deed pursuant to this Section shall grant any rights or any expectancy interest in the approval of the Master Deed. b. Expiration of Site Plan Approval If construction has not commenced, or if the project has commenced but has not made reasonable progress, within twelve (12) months after final approval of the site plan, the site plan approval expires and a new application for site plan review shall be required. However, the applicant may apply in writing to the Township Board for an extension of site plan approval, whereupon the Township Board may seek the Planning Commission's recommendation. The Township Board may grant one or more extensions of up to twelve (12) months upon request from the applicant prior to expiration of the previous approval and provided that it finds that the approved site plan adequately represents current conditions on and surrounding the site and provided that the site plan conforms to current Zoning Ordinance standards. c. Application for Certificate of Occupancy Following completion of site work and building construction, the applicant may apply for a Certificate of Occupancy or a Temporary Certificate of Occupancy from the Building Inspector in accordance with the procedures set forth in Section 29.07. It shall be the applicant's responsibility to obtain these required certificates prior to any occupancy of the property. d. Property Maintenance After Approval It shall be the responsibility of the owner of a property for which site plan approval has been granted to maintain the property in accordance with the approved site design on a continuing basis until the property is razed, or until new zoning regulations supersede the regulations upon which site plan approval was based, or until a new site design is approved. Any property owner who fails to so maintain an approved site design shall be deemed in violation of the use provisions of this Ordinance and shall be subject to the same penalties appropriate for a use violation. Williamstown Township Zoning Ordinance Page 29 - 4 Article 29.00 General Procedures and Related Standards With respect to condominium projects, the Master Deed shall contain provisions describing the responsibilities of the condominium association, condominium owners, and public entities, with regard to maintenance of the property in accordance with the approved site plan on a continuing basis. The Master Deed shall further establish the means of permanent financing for required maintenance and improvement activities which are the responsibility of the condominium association. Failure to maintain an approved site plan shall be deemed in violation of the use provisions of this Ordinance and shall be subject to the same penalties appropriate for a use violation. e. Monuments Requirements for Condominium Projects All condominium projects shall be marked with monuments as required by Condominium Rules promulgated to the Michigan Department of Commerce, Corporation and Securities Bureau, and as may also be required by the Township Engineer pursuant to engineering standards enforced by the Township of Williamstown. f. Recorded and As-Built Condominium Documents Upon approval of the site plan for a condominium project involving new construction, the condominium project developer or proprietor shall furnish the Township with the following: (1) One (1) copy of the recorded Master Deed, and (2) One (1) copy of any Condominium Bylaws and restrictive covenants. (3) One (1) copy of the recorded Condominium Subdivision Plan (Exhibit B). Upon completion of the project, the condominium project developer or proprietor shall furnish the Township with two (2) copies of an "as built survey". The as-built survey shall be reviewed by the Township Engineer for compliance with Township Ordinances. Fees for this review shall be established by the Township Board. 9. Site Plan Violation In the event that construction is not in compliance with the approved plans, the Building Inspector shall issue a “stop work” order until corrective action is taken or a revised site plan is submitted for Township review, following the normal site plan review procedures in Section 29.02. If the builder or developer fails to take corrective action or pursue approval of an amended site plan, the Building Inspector may issue a citation, after which the Township Board may commence and pursue appropriate action in a court having jurisdiction. 10. Modification to Approved Plan Minor modifications to an approved site plan may be reviewed by the Township Building Inspector or Township Engineer. a. Minor Modification Defined Minor modifications are changes that do not substantially affect the character or intensity of the use, vehicular or pedestrian circulation, drainage patterns, the demand for public services, or the danger from hazards. Examples of minor modifications include: 1) 2) 3) 4) An addition to an existing commercial or industrial building that does not increase or decrease the floor space by more than twenty-five percent (25%) or two thousand (2,000) square feet, whichever is less. Re-occupancy of a vacant building that has been unoccupied for less than twelve (12) months. Changes to building height that do not add an additional floor. Alterations or modifications involving less than five (5) parking spaces. text: Donna Tocarchick fo a Outlook From: Donna Tocarchick Sent: Saturday, November 7, 2026 1:05 PM To: Sheryl Monette Subject: 11/10 meeting Attachments: ai data center info.docx | may not be able to make Tuesday's meeting. My input is listed below. In addition, I've done some more research on data center hum. | hada little "conversation" with Al about it. What I've attached is the results of that conversation. The first portion is general information and explanation of issues and potential corrections to those issues. The second part is an executive summary and some recommendations for text to be included in an ordinance. 1. On the capital improvement plan for township hall remodel, the "planning context" says it's part of an adopted policy program or plan. But there is no program policy or plan listed for it as required. 2. Regarding the capital improvement plan for the township community park engineering fees, it is listed as being state or federally mandated. | don't know why it is considered to be state or federally mandated. 3. In the data center regulations - page 10 paragraph (a) - forgot to take out the words "cooling system". Donna Unlike a light appliance vibration, data center noise is massive, complex, and industrial. It is a dual-layered acoustic problem caused by hundreds of high-powered cooling fans, massive HVAC chillers, and localized natural gas or diesel power generators running 24/7. Measuring and understanding the hum from a nearby data center involves two distinct types of noise pollution: 1. The Airborne Whine (Audible Noise) This is the high-pitched, loud "vacuum cleaner drone" that neighbors can hear directly through closed windows. The Culprits: Thousands of industrial servers processing Al workloads need extreme airflow, creating a multi-blade whine from exhaust fans. The Levels: In places like Dowagiac, Michigan, and Southaven, Mississippi, residents have recorded outdoor levels fluctuating between 71 and 75 decibels (dB), with some facilities peaking closer to 96 dB right near the property line. How to measure it: This can be captured easily with standard, calibrated type-2 sound level meters or smartphone decibel apps (like NIOSH SLM) to track violations against local daytime/nighttime industrial noise ordinances. 2. The Heavy Low-Frequency Thrum (Infrasound) This is the most insidious component—the deep, sub-audible physical vibration that residents report feeling as "pressure" in their chests or ears rather than a sound. The Culprits: Massive industrial chillers, rooftop cooling towers, and continuous-run on- site power turbines (such as the methane-powered turbines used at some facilities). The Impact: Because this noise falls below 20 Hz (Infrasound), it travels incredibly long distances, penetrates solid concrete walls, and bypasses the human ear entirely— vibrating the body and causing symptoms like vertigo, severe migraines, nausea, and insomnia. How to measure it: Standard sound meters and cell phones will read this as total silence because they filter out frequencies below 20 Hz. To legally prove infrasound is present, acoustic engineers must use microbarometers or specialized low-frequency linear microphones (like the ROGA Instruments) to plot the unweighted sound pressure spectrum. Legal and Community Pushback Data center operators (such as Alliance Cloud Services or Vantage Data Centers) are facing class- action lawsuits and mounting fines as towns rapidly pass emergency industrial noise ordinances. Many companies are being forced to build massive localized acoustic barrier walls, switch to liquid cooling, or even offer to buy out affected residential properties. Many municipalities are finding out the hard way that traditional industrial noise ordinances are completely inadequate for data centers. Standard zoning codes rely entirely on dBA (A-weighted decibels). Because dBA mimics the human ear by filtering out low frequencies, a data center can perfectly pass a 55 dBA property line limit while simultaneously emitting a massive, structural dBC (C-weighted) low-frequency hum that vibrates neighboring homes, prevents sleep, and drives residents mad. To protect your community and ensure the ordinance survives legal scrutiny, your framework must include the following structural sound protections: 1. Dual-Metric Limits (dBA + dBC) Do not allow the ordinance to measure only dBA. You must establish a "C-minus-A" trigger or explicit dBC caps to capture low-frequency HVAC rumble and chiller thrum. ¢ The Standard Cap Method: Set an absolute dual limit at the residential property line. For example, a strict but legally defensible framework (adapted from progressive municipal updates) is: o Daytime: Max 55 dBA/ 70 dBC o Nighttime: Max 45 dBA / 60 dBC ¢ The Delta Method: Alternatively, state that if the dBC reading exceeds the dBA reading by 15 or 20 dB, it automatically triggers an unweighted octave-band analysis for low- frequency violation. 2. Unweighted Octave-Band Limits (dBZ) A data center can sometimes stay under dBA and dBC limits but still emit a razor-sharp "pure tone" hum at a highly specific frequency (like 31.5 Hz or 63 Hz). e Your ordinance should require dBZ (unweighted) limits across the nine standard octave bands. e Ifa data center peaks sharply in even one isolated octave band, they are in violation. 3. Clear Definition of "Tonal Sound" & Penalties A continuous pure-tone hum is infinitely more aggravating to the human brain than random, ambient white noise (like wind or traffic). The Tonal Penalty: Include a clause stating that if the noise contains a "steady pure tone” (defined mathematically via ANSI/ISO standards as a narrow frequency band protruding 10 dB or more above adjacent bands), a 5 to 6 dB penalty is automatically added to their recorded measurement. This effectively forces them to operate 5 dB quieter if their equipment hums. 4. Mandatory "Worst-Case Scenario" Modeling A common loophole for developers is submitting an acoustical engineering study modeled under mild spring weather with minimal server loads. The ordinance text should explicitly mandate that all pre-development predictive sound modeling (such as CadnaA or SoundPLAN) must assume simultaneous maximum capacity operating conditions. This means modeling the facility during peak summer cooling demand (when chillers and exhaust fans scream at 100%) combined with the concurrent testing of emergency backup diesel generators. 5. Enforceable Measurement Protocols Do not relegate the measurement details to an administrative manual; put them directly in the text of the ordinance so they are legally binding. Specify: The Meter: Must be a Type 1 Precision Sound Level Meter (not a smartphone or cheap Type 2 meter). The Location: Measured at the property line of the receiving "Sensitive Receptor" (residential, school, hospital). The Metric: Use (Equivalent Continuous Sound Level) over a 10-minute or 1-hour window. Avoid simple averages, which allow intense bursts of noise to be mathematically hidden by quiet intervals. 6. Operational Restrictions on Maintenance * Generator Testing: Backup diesel generators are deafening. The ordinance should restrict routine generator maintenance and readiness testing strictly to daytime hours (e.g., weekdays only, between 10:00 AM and 4:00 PM) and limit testing to a maximum of 10 hours per month. SUBJECT: Crucial Acoustic Enhancements for the Draft Data Center Zoning Ordinance Executive Summary Traditional municipal noise ordinances rely exclusively on dBA (A-weighted decibels). This metric filters out low-frequency sounds to mimic the human ear. However, data centers emit massive, continuous low-frequency hums and structural vibrations from HVAC chillers, cooling towers, and thousands of internal server fans running 24/7. A data center can perfectly satisfy a 55 dBA property line limit while simultaneously generating an oppressive low-frequency thrum that causes severe sleep disturbance and distress for nearby residents. To insulate our township from severe enforcement loopholes and future litigation, we must integrate a modernized, multi-layered acoustic framework into our final ordinance. Core Recommendations for Ordinance Text 1. Implement Dual-Metric Limits (dBA + dBC) The ordinance must regulate both audible high-frequency noise (dBA) and heavy low-frequency noise (dBC). * Proposed Standard: Establish strict daytime and nighttime caps at the property line of any adjacent residential or sensitive zone. o Daytime (7:00 AM — 10:00 PM): Maximum 55 dBA / 70 dBC o Nighttime (10:00 PM - 7:00 AM): Maximum 45 dBA / 60 dBC * The Delta Trigger: Alternatively, include a clause stating that if the C-weighted sound level (ABC) exceeds the A-weighted sound level (dBA) by 15 dB or more, it automatically triggers mandatory unweighted octave-band testing. 2. Establish Unweighted Octave-Band Limits (dBZ) Data center equipment can isolate a "pure tone" hum at a precise frequency (typically 31.5 Hz or 63 Hz). Even if total noise levels remain below dBA/dBC caps, these isolated spikes are highly disruptive. The ordinance should mandate that sound pressure levels must not exceed specified maximums across the nine standard unweighted dBZ octave bands (from 31.5 Hz up to 8,000 Hz) at the property line.

text: CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF YORK BOARD OF TRUSTEES REGULAR MEETING MINUTES TUESDAY, OCTOBER 13, 2026, 7:00 P.M. The Charter Township of York Board of Trustees held a Regular Board Meeting called to order at 7:00 pm by Supervisor Ludwig. He then led the Pledge of Allegiance. Roll Call of Board Members: Jason McGovern, Tom Gary, Helen Neill, Sally Louis, Dave Ludwig, John Hargrove, and Kayleigh Zupi. Others Present: See list. Short Public Comments (three minutes or less): One heard. Written Petitions: None. CONSENT AGENDA C1 Approve the Charter Township of York Regular meeting minutes: September 8, 2026, as presented C2 Approve Disbursements: September 9, 2026 – October 13, 2026, as presented C3 Recognize reports from Clerk: September 2026 Revenue/Expenditures C4 Recognize Treasurer’s Report September 2026 C5 Recognize Board correspondence September 2026 C6 Recognize written report from Building Official/Zoning Administrator, September 2026 C7 Recognize written report from Assessor, month of September 2026 C8 Recognize written report from Zoning Code Enforcement Officer, Q3 C9 Recognize written report from Washtenaw County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO), month of August 2026 C 10 Approve plumbing permit refund request of $400 to Plumbco Moved by Louis, seconded by Zupi, to approve the October 13, 2026, Consent Agenda as presented. Discussion: None. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. REGULAR AGENDA Moved by Zupi, seconded by Hargrove, to approve the October 13, 2026, Regular Agenda as amended, removing Item 2 under Unfinished Business, York Township Public Safety Millage. Discussion: Supervisor Ludwig reported advice from Township counsel to defer a decision on the proposed millage reduction until after the election. A possible November 5, 2026, special meeting was discussed if the fire authority millage passes, to allow preparation of tax bills. Item 1, the fire authority budget, remained on the agenda. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. VERBAL REPORTS Cpl. Carter, Washtenaw County Sheriff’s Office – Reported no significant incidents in September. Activity included four animal complaints, one medical assist, three traffic crashes, and 41 traffic stops resulting in 13 citations. Staffing and officers in training were discussed. Mike Siefker, Building Official/Zoning Administrator – Reported two new houses in September and 604 permits year to date. The counting method now includes each permit, rather than only the shared project number. Reported 64 inspections and 11 plan reviews. Permits were issued for a long-dormant residential construction project to resume. BOARD REPORTS Trustee Hargrove – Milan Area Fire Department approved a $640,000 tanker purchase, which would substantially reduce its capital improvement fund. Grant assistance is being sought. York’s participation continues through June 30, 2027. Trustee Neill – No additional report. An Election Commission meeting is forthcoming. Treasurer Louis – Reported approximately 120 delinquent summer tax accounts; reminder notices have been sent. Clerk Zupi – Election preparation continues. The September 26, 2026, bulk waste event received positive feedback. Final disposal and tire totals and costs were pending; a fuller report will follow the Environmental Committee meeting. Trustee Gary – The Planning Commission had not yet held its October meeting because of the holiday schedule. A report will follow next month. Trustee McGovern – The Personnel Committee discussed job descriptions, qualifications, and compensation budgets for the digital outreach/social media and recording secretary positions, for presentation to the Board in November. Members also discussed acknowledging a neighbor’s mowing of Township property at Sandra Richardson Park, confirming boundaries and existing survey markers, and reviewing prior boundary records before considering additional surveying. Follow-up was discussed for after the election. Supervisor Ludwig – Reported on the Saline Area Fire Authority budget process and work on the fire chief and administrative assistant contracts. The Township received $21,100 from Washtenaw County Parks and Recreation for the non-motorized pathway and $151,900 as the second portion of the EGLE solar grant. Department and committee budget requests are being collected, with a preliminary budget targeted for January 1. A reported $5 fuel-related increase from Steven’s Disposal prompted a request to review the contract. Sanford Road work encountered loose sand requiring stabilization; possible additional costs and next year’s county road funding were discussed. UNFINISHED BUSINESS 1. Saline Area Fire Authority 2027 FY Budget Discussion: Members reviewed the requested township contribution for the 2027 fiscal year commencing January 1, 2027, and asked for the detailed operating budget. Supervisor Ludwig corrected the agenda amount from $1,188,030 to $1,153,207. Discussion addressed the funding arrangement if the millage fails, the continuing Milan obligation for January–June 2027, and the distinction between authorizing the Township’s representatives to support a proposed budget and directly approving expenditures. Moved by Louis, seconded by Zupi, to authorize Trustee John Hargrove and Supervisor Dave Ludwig to vote yes on the proposed Saline Area Fire Authority budget for fiscal year 2027, with York Township’s contribution of $1,153,207. Roll Call Vote: Aye: Hargrove, Neill, Louis, Ludwig, Zupi, Gary, McGovern Nay: None Abstain: None Absent: None Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Abstain: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. 2. York Township Public Safety Millage 3. Citizen Notifications & Alerts Moved by Louis, seconded by Zupi, to accept the Citizen Notifications & Alerts proposal from GoGov, LLC, including the texting option, at $4,680 per year plus approximately $1,000 for texting, and authorize the Supervisor to sign. Discussion: The first-year cost was clarified as approximately $5,680. Members discussed record retention and retrieval, designated operator responsibilities, approval by two authorized Township officials before publication, and completion of the job description and policy for November Board review. The setup estimate was clarified as four to six weeks. Volunteer onboarding assistance and including sign-up information with winter tax bills were discussed. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. NEW BUSINESS 1. Partial Release of Performance Guarantee Moved by Zupi, seconded by Neill, to accept the request by Jacob Iacoangeli on behalf of Toll Brothers to release $2,825,487.00 of the $3,075,487.00 performance guarantee for the private roads in Phases 3 and 4 of Fosdick Glen, based on the schedule of completed work dated September 1, 2026, as recommended by Steve Sutton in the Township engineering consultant’s review email dated September 21, 2026. Discussion: Members clarified that $250,000 would remain as the guarantee and discussed its retention for two years after road completion. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. 2. Township Hall Sign Moved by McGovern, seconded by Zupi, to accept the Fastsigns proposal for a Township Hall sign, as presented or revised to comply with the Township zoning ordinance, at a cost not to exceed $6,800. Discussion: Members reviewed competing proposals, materials, placement, size, and zoning requirements. Supervisor Ludwig will work with Mike Siefker and the vendor on a compliant size and keep the Board informed before finalizing the sign. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. 3. Cyber Liability Coverage Moved by Louis, seconded by McGovern, to approve cyber liability coverage Option 2 for a prorated expense not to exceed $2,873. Discussion: Members discussed increased coverage and protection of resident information. The premium would be prorated from the actual coverage start date, rather than charging the full annual amount. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Motion carried. Public Comments (five minutes or less): None. Adjourn Moved by Neill, seconded by McGovern, to adjourn the Regular Board meeting at 8:12 p.m. Discussion: None. Voice Vote: Aye: 7; Nay: 0; Absent: 0. Canal Rd., north of W. Mt. Hope Hwy. (Parcel #040-022-300083-00). Applicant Michiana Land Investment, LLC has submitted a Special Land Use Permit (SLUP) application to establish a planned unit development (PUD) for the proposed Echo Valley East residential development. Echo Valley East would be a single-family detached site condominium development comprised of 63 lots located on 30.16 acres immediately east of the existing Echo Valley neighborhood on the east side of S. Canal Rd., north of W. Mt. Hope Hwy. The property is zoned RB (Single-Family - Low Density). The requested PUD would allow for a reduction in lot size, lot coverage, and building setbacks in exchange for the preservation of at least 25 percent of the total site as open space. In addition to the SLUP, Site Plan Review approval is required to move ahead with the project. The applicant has indicated they will apply for that process following a decision on the SLUP application. The Planning Commission held a public hearing and voted 5-0 to recommend approval of the SLUP at its meeting on November 9, 2026, citing the following reasons for its decision: 1. 2. 3. The Special Land Use Permit standards outlined in Section 7.03 of the Zoning Ordinance have been met. The general standards for review for Planned Unit Developments in Section 5.03 have been met. The specific use standards for condominium subdivisions in Section 8.17 of the Zoning Ordinance have been met. The Planning Commission recommended approval of the SLUP with the following conditions: 1. 2. 3. Approval is granted in accordance with the site plan prepared by Rowe Professional Services Company dated September 22, 2026, subject to the following revisions: a. A detail shall be provided showing the allowable locations of accessory buildings and attached decks as they related to the proposed building envelopes on each lot. b. The phase line differentiating between Phase 1 and Phase 2 shall be corrected to more clearly show which lots are in which phase. c. The lot frontages for Lots 14 and 15 shall be shown. Any modification or expansion of the use shall require approval of an amendment to the SLUP. The project shall receive Site Plan Review approval prior to the issuance of building permit(s). Prior to final Site Plan Review approval of the PUD, an Open Space Agreement shall be provided to the Township Board by the developer to ensure preservation and maintenance of the open space areas. Failure of the applicant to comply with any of the provisions required by the Zoning Ordinance, or any stipulations required by the Delta Township Board, shall constitute grounds for termination of this permit by the Delta Township Board. Scott Hendrickson Supervisor, Meridian Township hendrickson@meridian.mi.us 5151 Marsh Road | Okemos, MI 48864 From: Elizabeth Seagull Sent: Monday, November 9, 2026 11:26 AM To: Board <Board@meridian.mi.us> Subject: Invasive Plants in front of Meridian Township Service Center November 9, 2026 Dear Meridian Township Board, As we just saw in the resounding support for the renewal of the Parks Millage, Meridian Township residents love and value our parks and natural areas. As it happens, I was working the recent election as an election inspector helping Precinct 10 voters. We were located at the Meridian Township Service Center (Parks and Recreation). Given that Emma Campbell, her team and volunteers are working hard to remove invasive plant species from our parks and natural areas and plant locally native species, I found the choice of plantings in front of the building inappropriate. Township residents may innocently believe that the planting directly framing the Meridian Township Service Center where Parks and Recreation is housed represents a model planting. This is far from the case. I saw Chinese silver grass (Miscanthus sinensis) in a prominent position, with variegated Vinca major, also known as periwinkle myrtle, as a groundcover. Both of these species have become invasive in natural areas, although they are not yet listed by MDARD. There may be other invasive plants in that foundation planting that frames the building entrance that I was not able to identify due to season dormancy. We all know that invasive species are a huge issue in our township. I took a short walk during a brief break on November 3 into the trailhead of Central Park South/Nancy Moore Park and was dismayed at the large number of invasive shrubs growing there, especially aggressive Eurasian honeysuckles (Lonicera spp.). Changing the plantings in front of the Meridian Township Service Center would be a much smaller project than tackling the nearby trails. Both are important. But I propose that all the plantings around township-owned buildings should be models showcasing the beautiful and beneficial plants native to our area that support our precious local ecosystem. Please consider giving this a high priority in the coming year. Thank you so much for continuing to support planting a native Meridian. Sincerely, Elizabeth A. COMMUNICATIONS Principal Planner Shorkey discussed the communication from the Tri-County Regional Planning Commission. After discussion, Principal Planner Shorkey said that he would add the resolution to support the Middle Grand River Water Trail state designation to the next agenda. Vice-Chair McCurtis arrived during the discussion at 6:33. 7. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. SUP #26035 – Bridges Child Care Page 1 Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet. Principal Planner Shorkey complimented the application and showed the plan in the packet. Commissioner Nahum said that this was a good location and strongly supported the application. Principal Planner Shorkey said that based on the conversation, Staff would bring a resolution to recommend approval to the next meeting. 8. UNFINISHED BUSINESS A. PUD #26026 – Capstone Hannah Boulevard Apartments Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet and said that based on the public hearing, a resolution to approve was in the packet. Principal Planner Shorkey complemented the Applicants for their interaction with the public. Commissioner Nahum agreed with Principal Planner Shorkey and complemented the Applicants for their public interaction. Commissioner Brooks discussed the application and raised concern about the amount of parking on the plan, noting environmental issues, transit issues, the cost of parking passed on to residents, and the incentivization of parking. Commissioner Brooks said that he would vote yes but that the issue of parking should be looked at for future developments. Commissioner McConnell asked about conditions in the resolution and said discussed Commissioner Brooks’ comments. Commissioner Nahum moved to adopt the resolution recommending approval of Planned Unit Development #26026 to allow for the construction of 256 new multiple-family homes on approximately 69 acres located on Hannah Parkway, subject to the conditions found in the resolution to approve. Seconded by Vice-Chair McCurtis. Motion passed unanimously. B. SUP #26028 – New Hope Church Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet and said that based on the public hearing, a resolution to approve was in the packet. Vice-Chair McCurtis moved to adopt the resolution recommending approval of Special Use Permit #26028 to expand the church sanctuary, enlarge the parking lot, and construct new sidewalks and classrooms at 6482 Newton Road. Seconded by Commissioner Nahum. Motion passed unanimously. C. ZA #26025 – Professional Office Updates Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet and said that based on the public hearing, a resolution to approve was in the packet. Page 2 Commissioner Brooks moved to adopt the resolution recommending approval of Zoning Amendment #26025 in accordance with the revised draft ordinance language. Seconded by Commissioner McConnell. Motion passed unanimously. Chair Romback explained the text amendment and the reasoning behind it to the students in the audience. 9. OTHER BUSINESS A. ZA #26039 – Data Center Amendment – Discussion (Discussed after Item B) Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo, pointed out the draft ordinance, and discussed the history of the proposal. Principal Planner Shorkey said that there was no potential data center application nor was Staff in conversation with any potential data center applicant. Principal Planner Shorkey said that the Township Attorney would be at the November 16 meeting and that he was there to collect questions. Commissioner McConnell said that the draft ordinance includes requirements about a decommissioning plan and asked if there are any other uses in the zoning ordinance that require a decommissioning plan. Chair Romback suggested that the full cost to decommission a data center should be required up front before a data center is approved. Vice-Chair McCurtis asked if it is possible to simply outright ban data centers. Commissioner Nahum discussed data center approval processes and said that the State could allow one if a local municipality does not have an approval process. Discussion about data center projects. Commissioner Nahum said that the Board wanted a response on the draft ordinance by the end of the year. Vice-Chair McCurtis asked how restrictive the Planning Commission could be. Commissioner McConnell said that on first reading, the draft ordinance addresses typical concerns. Commissioner Nahum asked if there examples of data center ordinance from other communities. Chair Romback discussed cost neutrality and asked if the ordinance be drafted to get “cost neutrality” to residents. Commissioner McConnell asked what the difference is between a closed loop cooling system versus a recycled water system. Chair Romback asked for the study for the community impact analysis to be an independent study paid for by the applicant. Discussion about development reviews, after which Chair Romback suggested adding the word “independent.” Principal Planner Shorkey showed the Township zoning map and showed where the Industrial zoning areas are. Commissioner McConnell discussed the uses on Dawn Avenue and suggested a data center might not be out of place. Commissioner Nahum discussed sizes of data centers and said that he was worried that it would over regulate and asked what is the minimum size for a data center to be regulated. Commissioner Brooks discussed data centers and asked if the ordinance too restrictive and limiting potential business opportunities. Commissioner Brooks suggested allowing data centers or BESS in the PO district. Commissioner Brooks said that the draft ordinance feels so restrictive as to prohibit development of data centers and asked if different sizes of data centers were looked at when drafting the ordinance. Page 3 Commissioner McConnell discussed server rooms and said that businesses in professional offices can exceed 50 square feet. Commissioner McConnell said that he wanted to hear more about what current operations have for current data centers and brought up the Delta Dental building as an example. Commissioner Nahum suggest that the Planning Commission does not want to impact existing systems. Discussion about current systems and how to define different data centers. Chair Romback asked if there are any model data center ordinances. Principal Planner Shorkey said not yet. Commissioner Nahum asked if data centers can be regulated by data usage and 50 square foot is way too small. Commissioner Brooks asked about proposed data center requirements and asked what other projects have similar requirements. Commissioner Brooks discussed the requirement for a “Threat Assessment and Risk Mitigation” and said that he was not interested in the proposed surveillance requirements. Further discussion about proposed data center regulations. Commissioner Brooks asked about electromagnetic interference and asked if could be more restrictive; there is an option for applicants to describe why they cannot meet requirements, but can the ordinance say that applicants must meet requirements. Commissioner McConnell suggested deleting language allowing applicants options and that electromagnetic interference be grounds for denial. Commissioner Nahum asked about noise restrictions and asked if there is existing language regulation decibels and suggested that 55 decibels is not restrictive enough. Commissioner Brooks asked if the standards as written apply to data centers and BESS. Commissioner Brooks asked if BESS are only acceptable attached to a data center. Chair Romback asked if there is a fire at a data center, is Meridian Township Fire in a position to handle today. Chair Romback suggested that if the risk assessment indicates that equipment upgrades are necessary for Township agencies, we make the applicant fund that equipment upgrade. Principal Planner Shorkey said that he would schedule a public hearing for the proposed amendment for the November 16 Planning Commission agenda. B. ZA #26040 – Hard Cider Production in the RR District – Discussion (Discussed before Item A) Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo and discussed the history of the proposed text amendment. Vice-Chair McCurtis asked if hard cider was alcoholic and if it required an alcoholic permit. Principal Planner Shorkey introduced the applicant to discuss licensing procedures. Chair Romback asked if the floor should be opened and discussed procedure and opened the floor to the applicants. Mr. Keenan Gibbons and Mr. Sam DeKamp spoke about the application. Mr. DeKamp said that the license would be a small wine maker license and required municipal approval and zoning compliance. Principal Planner Shorkey pointed out the proposed conditions. Commissioner Brooks discussed Burgdorf Winery and asked about that township’s ordinances. Commissioner Brooks asked about Red Cedar Distillery. Principal Planner Shorkey discussed the differences between the proposed cider facility and Bergdorf and Red Cedar. Page 4 Sam DeKamp discussed the differences between distilling and hard cider and said that hard cider is considered wine by the State. Mr. Gibbons noted that the conditions prohibit public consumption and Mr. DeKamp said that public consumption was not his intent. Commissioner Nahum asked if this was allowed by right in the Agricultural district; further discussion about the Agriculture district. Commissioner Brooks said that this activity is happening around the Township and that he sees no issue with the amendment and pointed out other agricultural businesses. Chair Romback agreed and suggested that the proposed conditions are too restrictive. Commissioner McConnell agreed and asked about the history of the apples on the property. After discussion, Commissioner McConnell asked about the expected production. Mr. DeKamp said that he is processing about 800 pounds of apples, hoping to increase to thousands of pounds but would need to grow more apples. Commissioner McConnell asked what happened to the byproducts. Mr. Gibbons said that they were working with EGLE and that it would act as compost and fertilizer. Mr. DeKamp further discussed the waste process. Mr. Gibbons asked if the draft could still be changed based on the discussion. Principal Planner Shorkey said the Planning Commission could make suggestions. Chair Romback discussed the conditions and suggested potential changes. Commissioner Nahum suggested removing restrictions for tasting rooms. After discussion, Principal Planner Shorkey suggested that tasting rooms sounded appropriate, based on the conversation, but that restaurants and event centers were too intense for the intent. Commissioner Brooks asked about the time frame for the applicants. Commissioner Brooks asked about other uses for the public and asked for a potential scope of activities. Commissioner Brooks asked Principal Planner Shorkey to discuss current business uses allowed in the Rural Residential district. Commissioner Nahum suggested striking sections E through I from the proposed conditions and adding some of the struck subjects as Special Uses. Chair Romback asked for another discussion of the draft amendment before a public hearing. Commissioner Brooks agreed and asked Principal Planner Shorkey about Township alcohol licensing. Discussion about next steps ensued. Commissioner Brooks asked for related information from Williamston Township. After discussion, Principal Planner Shorkey said that he would include the proposed amendment, reflecting the proposed changes, on the November 16 Planning Commission agenda for further discussion. 10. REPORTS AND ANNOUNCEMENTS A. Township Board Update Principal Planner Shorkey updated the Planning Commission on recent Board activity and said that a new Planning Commissioner was joining the Commission in December. B. Liaison Reports Commissioner Nahum said that the Zoning Board of Appeals had nothing to report. Page 5 11. PROJECT UPDATES Principal Planner Shorkey said that the project report had one update and said that he attended the ribbon cutting for BB.Q Chicken. 12. PUBLIC REMARKS None 13. COMMISSIONER COMMENTS None. 14. ADJOURNMENT Chair Romback called for a motion to adjourn the meeting. Commissioner Nahum moved to adjourn the October 26, 2026 regular meeting of the Planning Commission. Seconded by Vice-Chair McCurtis. Motion passed unanimously at 8:24. Page 6 To: Planning Commission From: Timothy R. Schmitt, AICP Community Planning and Development Director Date: November 13, 2026 Re: Ordinance 2026-14 – Data Center and Battery Energy Storage Systems regulations After the initial discussion, the Planning Commission had a number of questions related to the ordinance. Staff will respond to some in this memo and the Township Attorney will be prepared to discuss the remainder at the Planning Commission’s meeting on Monday, November 16. To reiterate a point I’ve made continuously this year, there is no proposal for a data center or a BESS project, nor has Staff had any discussions with anyone that would give any inkling there is a project being considered. This ordinance is purely proactive, intending to get regulations in place, in the event that a project comes together. - - The draft ordinance includes requirements about a decommission plan. Are there any other uses in the zoning ordinance that require a decommission plan? If not, why not? – There are no other uses that explicitly require a decommissioning plan. However, Wireless Facilities are required to post funding to allow for removal if the site is abandoned. Is it possible to simply outright ban data centers? – As a general rule, you cannot outright ban any use in the State of Michigan. Are there examples of data center ordinance from other communities? – There are some, but generally, we are in a period where everyone is drafting ordinances specific to their communities on this issue, so looking to our colleagues is less helpful than usual. What is the difference between a closed loop cooling system versus a recycled water system? – The closed loop cooling system refers specifically to a system where water is continually recycled to cool equipment. A recycled water system is a broader definition, which could refer to other uses of water (irrigation and sanitation being other options). Can the ordinance define different sizes of data centers? – Certainly, but the initial thought was to only have two categories, so as not to try and arbitrarily define the size of a facility that we may or may not permit in the Township. By not splitting it further, we create a more defensible ordinance. What current places in the Township exceed 50 square feet? – They exist throughout the Township, but we don’t have a comprehensive list. Staff and the Township Attorney have discussed how to not impact existing facilities and we will continue to work on that issue going forward. Where did the 50 square feet requirement come from. – This was a starting point to define the term and can be changed, if the Planning Commission believes it should be higher. Making the threshold smaller is not viable, as nearly any computer equipment area would fall under the definition then. Providing a safe and welcoming, sustainable, prime community. Ordinance 2026-14 – Data Centers and BESS Page 2 - Do the standards as written apply to data centers and BESS? Are BESS only acceptable attached to a data center? – As written, BESS facilities would only be permitted in conjunction with a Data Center. The remaining questions that will be addressed by the Township Attorney include: - Can the ordinance be drafted to get “cost neutrality” to residents? - What is the minimum size for a data center? - Is the ordinance too restrictive and limiting potential business opportunities? What about allowing data centers or BESS in the PO district? - There was some discussion about how to define different data centers. Can they be regulated by purpose? - Why is the requirement for a “Threat Assessment and Risk Mitigation” included? - Can the language about electromagnetic interference be more restrictive? There is an options for applicants to describe why they can’t meet requirements, but can the ordinance say Must Meet? - If the risk assessment indicates that equipment upgrades are necessary for Township agencies, can we make the applicant fund that equipment upgrade? Staff looks forward to continuing this conversation with the Planning Commission. Should the Attachments 1. To provide for the adoption of supplementary rules and regulations and other matters related to the museum facilities owned by the Charter Township of Port Huron. Section 1. Title This Ordinance shall be known as the “Port Huron Charter Township Historical Commission Ordinance.” Section 2. Purpose The purpose of this Ordinance is to provide for the use, protection, regulation and control of the Museum facilities, areas, and other matters concerning historical preservation, education, and conservation. To provide for the adoption of supplementary rules and regulations and other matters related to the museum facilities owned by the Charter Township of Port Huron. Section 3. Establishment The Port Huron Charter Township Historical Commission is hereby established. Section 4. Membership The Historical Commission shall consist of five (5) members who shall be appointed by the Supervisor with the approval of the Township Board. Not more than two members may be Township Board members. Each member shall serve a term of 3 years. Historical Commission Members and volunteers are expected to follow the “Committee, Commission, & Board Commitment Standards” as established October 7, 2013 and the Historical Commission Agreement & Code of Ethics. Letters of interest of appointment as well as letters of resignation shall both be directed to the Township Supervisor. (Questionnaire located on Township Website) Section 5. Grounds for Removal Any member that violates the “Committee, Commission, & Board Commitment Standards and/or the Historical Commission Agreement & Code of Ethics may be removed from their seat on the Historical Commission by majority vote of the Township Board. Section 6. Officers, Meetings & Records A. The Historical Commission shall organize by annually electing a Chairperson, Vice Chairperson, Recording Secretary/Treasurer, and any other officers from its membership as it may deem necessary.

Stumbo Township Clerk Debbie Swanson Township Treasurer Stan Eldridge Date: November 3, 2026 To: Clerk’s Office CC: Brenda Stumbo, Supervisor From: Michael Saranen, Operation Manager Subject: Department Report (activities in October 2026) Activities: Ford Lake Dam (Hydro Station) General Operation Summary: The Hydro Station is operating safely and continues to get routine safety inspections and preventive maintenance. Operators had 1 after hour call-in(s) for the month for water levels. Average precipitation for the month of is around 2.53”, this year NOAA recorded it to be 2.05”. Regulatory Status: Items for 2026- DSSMR- Complete, Filed with FERC Owners Dam Safety Program Review/Update – Complete, Filed with FERC EAP annual update and test – Started EAP First Responder Training – Complete WQ Report - Draft Report in Review Nuisance Plant Plan Report – Complete, filed with FERC Wildlife Plan Report – Draft Report in Review Historical Activity Report – Complete, Filed Gate Certification – Started Security Review – Plan update and training done, FERC filing in October FERC Security Inspection – TBD FERC Annual Dam Safety Inspection – Complete Annual DEQ Lake Operation Monitoring Report- Complete, filed with FERC Periodic Items- Spillway Assessment Action Plan - Filed, addressing comments by FERC, Ongoing Public Safety Plan - No Actions needed at this time Fish & Sediment Analysis - Not required until 2033 Shoreline Erosion Survey – Not required until 2030 Emergency generator 4-year testing/maintenance – planned 2029 EAP Tabletop and Functional Exercise – 2029 EAP Rewrite – 2030 Owners Dam Safety Audit - 2030 2025 Part 12D Comprehensive Analysis – Started, next step Risk Analysis (final report due March 2027) Protective Relay testing – Due again 2031 Current Projects: Roof Replacement was approved by the Board in July, paperwork is now in order, and work is planned for November weather permitting. Concrete Repairs- Delayed, approved by the Board to go out to bid. Construction was planned for summer 2023, however the cost came in doubled and the project is on hold until funding is available. Our DOE grant is moving forward; negotiations have not started but hopefully this summer/fall. Staff are working on documentation updates in plans for a construction project in 2027. River Level Sensor Premature failure of this sensor has caused negative impact to the operation and emergency actions. Staff are working with engineers to fix the problem. In February, a radar style sensor was installed in parallel to the existing system. This new technology seems promising to help reduce the on-going cost and better system reliability. The testing period for the new sensor was planned for 60 days; this has been extended due to a defect in the sensor. No new information DTE/ITC Power Line Rebuild- ITC is planning a rebuild of the transmission line along Bridge Road. Project is planned in 2027 will likely take a couple of months to complete. We don’t know how this will impact Hydro’s operations. No New Information DTE Gas Line relocation- DTE has submitted plans to relocate the gas line attached to the bridge and dam. The project has easements now through North and South Hydro Parks. Construction was started in June 2026 and be completed in the fall. Future Maintenance Items: - Shoreline Restoration, Ford Lake Park PMF Study for watershed – on hold until Part 12 is complete Concrete repairs – On Hold, additional funding needed Windows/additional concrete repairs (powerhouse and dam) - TBD Sluice gate Repairs/Replacement- Sluice Gate Stress Analysis was done 2024, the FERC has requested a detailed study of the spillway gates. This is a common industry request from FERC as they continuously look at safety involving dams. The inspections were completed, and the engineer has identified some items for consideration. Making a plan of action. Water Quality Summary: MOU with City of Ann Arbor The Parties share a common interest in eliminating and preventing nuisance blue green algae blooms in Ford and Belleville Lakes, and they acknowledge that information about water quality and conditions in the lakes is important to advancing their common interest. THEREFORE, the Parties enter into this Memorandum of Understanding to memorialize their understanding as to their efforts to cooperate and work together to monitor, collect, and share water quality information regarding Ford and Belleville Lakes. Work Plan - for 2026, continue collecting data, follow updated discharge plan. Current Activities - The MOU team continues to have open discussions. Data is being reviewed, report forthcoming. Sluice Gate Usage Summary Releasing water from the sluice gates is primary done to maintain lake level when flow exceeds the powerhouse. At certain times, we can use the gates to help keep the lake mixed to maintain oxygen levels (effectiveness depends on several factors) at the bottom of the lake. The water quality monitoring begins on June 1st and will end on September 30th; operators monitor the water quality conditions and take readings as outlined in the WQ Plan. The dam releases water from the bottom gates to maintain run of river and/or help with the water quality in Ford Lake. The Federal License requires us to pass water with a minimum of 5mg/l of dissolved oxygen all the time. Therefore, spilling from the bottom gates in the summer to improve the lake is not always possible.
